docs.text: Tool What it does How to invoke desktop-control MCP Move mouse, click, key combos, screenshots mcp__desktop-control__move_mouse, __click, __key_combo App-specific skill Switch modes or toggle features in the app being demoed via AppleScript menus /<app> mode <name> (project-specific) AppleScript (direct) Any macOS UI automation — menu clicks, window focus, keystrokes osascript -e '...' Recordly Capture + auto-zoom + cursor polish + motion blur + styled frames (the "product-demo video" app) AGPL-3.0 desktop app; record → export MP4 → hand off to muriel's post-processing macOS built-in screen recording Zero-setup capture, no polish Cmd+Shift+5 — use when Recordly is overkill or unavailable ffmpeg (homebrew-ffmpeg tap) Trim, burn captions, add music, encode Hard-burn via subtitles filter (libass)

docs.title: With Recordly (recommended for polished product/walkthrough videos)
docs.text:
1. Record in Recordly — auto-zoom follows the cursor, cursor polish + motion blur applied in-editor, webcam overlay optional, styled frame around the final composition. Export MP4.
  2. (Optional) Burn captions via muriel — if you have a tooltip manifest with precise timecodes, run burn-tooltips.sh manifest.json recordly-out.mp4 final.mp4 to add hard-burned captions.
  3. (Optional) Further ffmpeg passes — trim, concat, encode for YouTube using the recipes below.

docs.title: Without Recordly (zero-setup path)
docs.text:
1. Write a tooltip manifest — JSON array of {start, end, text} objects
  2. Script the choreography — desktop-control moves the mouse on timed coordinates; AppleScript switches modes
  3. User records with Cmd+Shift+5 while agent drives the app
  4. Post-process: burn-tooltips.sh manifest.json raw.mov output.mp4
  5. Generates SRT from manifest
  6. Burns captions via ffmpeg subtitles filter (Helvetica 24px, white, black outline)
  7. Trims with -ss / -t flags
  8. Drops audio with -an when needed
  9. H.264 CRF 22, faststart for YouTube

docs.title: ffmpeg setup
docs.text:
The default brew install ffmpeg lacks drawtext/subtitles filters. Install the full version: 

brew uninstall ffmpeg
brew tap homebrew-ffmpeg/ffmpeg
brew install homebrew-ffmpeg/ffmpeg/ffmpeg
This includes freetype, libass, fontconfig — enables drawtext, subtitles, and ass filters.

docs.title: Tooltip burn script
docs.text:
A burn-tooltips.sh script (see your app repo or muriel/tools/) — two modes: 

# SRT only (no ffmpeg needed)
burn-tooltips.sh tooltips.json output.srt

# Full pipeline: trim + burn + optional music
burn-tooltips.sh tooltips.json raw.mov output.mp4 [music.mp3]

Uses subtitles filter (libass) for hard-burn. Falls back to soft-sub mux if drawtext unavailable. Music mixed at 15% volume.

docs.title: Lessons learned
docs.text:
• Trim first, caption second — tooltip timecodes are relative to the trimmed video, not the raw recording. Use -ss to skip dead intro before the filter chain.
  • Drop audio with -an — screen recordings capture system audio, dogs barking, etc.
  • macOS filenames have Unicode spaces — PM in screen recording filenames uses a narrow no-break space (U+202F). Use glob matching, not exact strings.
  • Excalidraw: skip hand-drawn — use roughness: 0, fontFamily: 2 (Helvetica), fillStyle: "solid". The hand-drawn aesthetic reads as fake, not charming.
  • SRT for YouTube — even with hard-burned captions, upload the SRT too. YouTube auto-translates it.

docs.title: ffmpeg editing recipes
docs.text:
Standalone operations for cutting, joining, and splitting video outside the tooltip pipeline.

# Cut segment (fast, keyframe-aligned)
ffmpeg -ss 00:00:10 -to 00:00:30 -i input.mp4 -c copy output.mp4

# Cut segment (precise, re-encodes)
ffmpeg -ss 00:00:10 -i input.mp4 -t 20 -c:v libx264 -c:a aac output.mp4

# Last N seconds
ffmpeg -sseof -30 -i input.mp4 -c copy output.mp4

# Concatenate via file list (recommended — works across codecs)
# list.txt contains: file 'clip1.mp4'\nfile 'clip2.mp4'\nfile 'clip3.mp4'
ffmpeg -f concat -safe 0 -i list.txt -c copy output.mp4

# Concatenate with re-encode (when codecs differ)
ffmpeg -f concat -safe 0 -i list.txt -c:v libx264 -c:a aac output.mp4

# Split into fixed-length segments
ffmpeg -i input.mp4 -c copy -f segment -segment_time 60 -reset_timestamps 1 output_%03d.mp4

-c copy vs re-encode: -c copy is instant but cuts on keyframes (may be off by a few frames). Add -c:v libx264 -c:a aac for frame-accurate cuts at the cost of speed. -ss before -i is faster; after -i is more precise.

docs.title: Design doc
docs.text: See docs/PERMUTE.md for the infographic aspiration: Tufte, Bertin, Gestalt, CRAP, semantic zoom, small multiples, linked displays.

docs.title: HTML → MP4 via hyperframes
docs.text:
For videos whose source of truth is HTML (release announcements, feature explainers, animated data viz, kinetic-typography compositions, website-to-video), use hyperframes (HeyGen, Apache 2.0). Puppeteer + FFmpeg + GSAP rendering; deterministic (same input → same output). Explicitly built for agent-driven authoring.

Installed globally via npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes -y -g. Registers five Claude Code slash commands:

Skill What it does /hyperframes HTML composition authoring — captions, TTS, audio-reactive animation, transitions /hyperframes-cli CLI commands — init, lint, preview, render, transcribe, tts, doctor /hyperframes-registry Block and component installation via hyperframes add <block> /website-to-hyperframes Capture a URL → turn it into a video (Scrutinizer.app promo candidate) /gsap GSAP timelines, easing, ScrollTrigger, framework integration, performance

docs.title: When to pick what
docs.text: If the source of truth is… Use A running macOS app (Scrutinizer mode sweeps, Psychodeli visualizer playback) Recordly An HTML composition (release demo, explainer, animated chart) hyperframes A scripted walkthrough driving a real app via the mouse desktop-control + ffmpeg A static screenshot pipeline that needs motion frosting (zoom-pan, fade-in caption) ffmpeg filters directly

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
npx hyperframes init my-video      # scaffolds HTML composition
cd my-video
npx hyperframes preview            # live-reload in browser
npx hyperframes render             # MP4 out

Compose in HTML with data attributes:

<div id="stage" data-composition-id="release" data-start="0" data-width="1920" data-height="1080">
  <video src="scrutinizer-demo.mp4" data-start="0" data-duration="8" data-track-index="0" muted playsinline></video>
  <div class="caption" data-start="1" data-duration="4" data-track-index="1">
    Only 2° of your vision is sharp.
  </div>
  <audio src="music.wav" data-start="0" data-duration="8" data-track-index="2" data-volume="0.5"></audio>
</div>

docs.title: Catalog blocks worth knowing
docs.text:
50+ prebuilt blocks at hyperframes.heygen.com/catalog:

  • Social overlays — instagram-follow, lower thirds, subscribe animations
  • Shader transitions — flash-through-white, WebGL dissolves
  • Data viz — data-chart (animated bar/line), counters
  • Captions + TTS — synced text over video, auto-narration
  • Audio-reactive — shaders or CSS animations driven by waveform analysis

Install blocks via npx hyperframes add <block-name>.

docs.title: Frame Adapter pattern
docs.text: Bring your own animation runtime (GSAP, Lottie, CSS, Three.js). PixiJS (vocabularies/pixijs.md) and kinetic-typography compositions should drop in via a custom adapter.

docs.title: Not a replacement
docs.text: hyperframes sits alongside the ffmpeg + Recordly + desktop-control recipes above, not instead of them. Pick the substrate by where the truth lives. A Scrutinizer feature demo video has three parts — a screen recording of the running app (Recordly), title cards and captions (hyperframes), and final encoding (ffmpeg). Stack them.

docs.title: Anti-patterns
docs.text:
• Don't capture with system audio on unless narration is intentional. Dogs bark, notifications ding, system alerts leak into shipped reels.
  • Don't burn subtitles in the default SRT font. Use the brand's typography so captions feel authored, not tacked on.
  • Don't edit at 30 fps then upload at 60 (or vice versa). Match the recording's frame rate or re-encode deliberately.
  • Don't ship a demo whose first 3 seconds don't hook attention. The opening frame is most of the commitment decision.

docs.title: Web — editorial HTML and static capture
docs.text:
Use this channel for prose-led web artifacts, Marginalia pages, Markdown-to-HTML or PDF pipelines, and browser-rendered stills. Use interactive.md when the reader manipulates the artifact; use polish.md for tactile product UI.

When a claim, value, or named entity benefits from an adjacent history or profile, consult the sparkline repertoire. Choose inline, margin, or table placement for the reading task; preserve the anchor through wrapping and carry scale context into static exports.

docs.title: Purpose in the solution
docs.text:
Make the content hierarchy, reading path, responsive behavior, and export path part of the implementation—not a decorative pass after the page works.

Before editing, tell the calling agent:

  • Purpose: which reading or presentation problem this channel will solve.
  • Integration: which existing content, component, or build path it will preserve.
  • Proof: which rendered viewport, contrast audit, or export will verify it.

docs.title: Default workflow
docs.text:
1. Identify the audience, primary reading task, and destination: live page, self-contained HTML, PNG, or PDF.
  2. Inspect the existing content and design tokens before choosing a visual register.
  3. Put the core narrative inline. Use sidebars and margin notes only for optional depth.
  4. Implement semantic HTML, a readable measure, responsive behavior, and keyboard-visible links and controls.
  5. Render the real page, inspect at representative widths, and run the contrast audit.
  6. Report the web decision that changed, the code or artifact carrying it, and the rendered evidence.

docs.title: High-leverage rules
docs.text:
• Keep body prose near 65–75ch; never center-align paragraphs.
  • Keep all text at Muriel's 8:1 floor. Demote with size, weight, and space—not opacity.
  • Use a deliberate typeface and palette; avoid pure #000/#fff, default gradient heroes, and repeated-card filler.
  • Keep essential content in the main flow. One optional aside per section is a useful ceiling.
  • Preserve semantic heading order, landmarks, focus visibility, and reduced motion.
  • Never hotlink placeholder imagery. Use local, generated, or embedded assets.
  • Wait for fonts before capture and verify the actual DOM width rather than a screenshot crop.
  • Animate transform and opacity, never layout properties.

docs.title: Choose the build path
docs.text: Need Path Editorial page with callouts Marginalia HTML/CSS Markdown that must fan out to HTML/PDF/DOCX Pandoc + Marginalia Lua filter Highly customized single-target explainer marginalia-md.js + project build script Browser page frozen to PNG Playwright or muriel.capture HTML converted to paged PDF WeasyPrint One portable file Data-URI embedding, within a deliberate size budget

docs.title: Minimal Marginalia setup
docs.text:
<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/marginalia@latest/marginalia.css">
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/marginalia@latest/marginalia.js" defer></script>

Use mg- classes and --mg-* tokens. Pick one document theme—OLED dark or warm editorial light—and keep figures in the same register.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
python -m muriel.contrast path/to/page.html
python -m muriel.capture https://example.com --dir captures/
weasyprint page.html page.pdf

Inspect at least one narrow and one wide viewport, keyboard traversal, console errors, overflow, image loading, and final export dimensions.

docs.title: Load deeper only when needed
docs.text: Read ../references/web-recipes.md only for exact Marginalia syntax, Pandoc transforms, light-editorial tokens, capture recipes, or data-URI implementation details. Do not load it for routine product UI work.

docs.title: muriel gallery
docs.text:
Worked examples from shipped projects that exemplify what muriel's channels produce. Each entry leads with the tool chain — which muriel helpers (and external libraries) produced the artifact. The goal is to make the abstract channel categories executable: if you want output like this, here's the exact recipe.

For the interactive in-browser set — 3D spatial typography, data mountains, the perspective wall — see the live spatial demos ↗.

docs.title: 0. muriel's own hero mark — Raster + Kinetic Typography + Visible Language
docs.text:
Tools: Pillow (still frame composition) · a custom 12-pose renderer (iterates frame_0..frame_11.png) · ffmpeg or ImageMagick convert -delay -loop 0 (GIF assembly) · muriel.contrast.audit_svg (8:1 text-rule check before ship). Channels: raster, svg, video. Vocabularies: visible-language (Cooper's mitp colophon reinterpreted), kinetic-typography (strategic motion, max contrast). Pattern: same mark, four variants — still + animated × light + dark — served via <picture> + prefers-color-scheme. Assets at assets/.

The rest of the gallery points at other shipped work that exemplifies each channel in its own right. Source blog posts live under the Scrutinizer dev log; this gallery references them, it doesn't host them.

docs.title: 1. Before / after comparison panel — Raster
docs.text: Tools: Pillow (image composition + draw) · matplotlib (curve overlay rendered as PNG, then composited) · muriel/typeset.py (caption typography) · muriel/contrast.py (pre-ship 8:1 audit). Channel: channels/raster.md. Pattern: canonical small-multiples A/B — identical framing, variable stimulus. Live: Color sprint →

docs.title: 2. Mode comparison — Raster (interactive → captured)
docs.text: Tools: a WebGL foveation engine (external, Scrutinizer) for the rendering · muriel/capture.py (capture_responsive() for retina screenshots) · Pillow (side-by-side composition) · muriel/dimensions.py (OG_CARD for final size). Channel: channels/raster.md (captured from channels/interactive.md). Pattern: same stimulus, two processing modes — small multiples across a parameter axis. Live: v2.6 release notes →

docs.title: 3. Reading-span A/B — Science
docs.text: Tools: matplotlib (figure composition with two subplot panels, body-text rendering via ax.text() or imported image, degree-of-visual-angle guides as axvline) · muriel/matplotlibrc_dark.py (palette + rcparams) · muriel/dimensions.py (figsize_for('chi', columns=2)) · muriel/stats.py (format_comparison() for the effect-size caption). Channel: channels/science.md. Pattern: paired-conditions comparison with labeled axes, effect size, and sample size — exactly what muriel.stats.format_comparison() formats into a figure caption. Live: Reading span on/off →

docs.title: 4. Saliency vs. congestion — Science
docs.text: Tools: matplotlib (dense small-multiples grid, GridSpec or subplot_mosaic) · numpy / polars (derived metric computation) · muriel/matplotlibrc_dark.py · muriel/dimensions.py (figsize_for('chi', columns=2) for IEEE/CHI venue width). Channel: channels/science.md. Pattern: stacked small-multiples for visual diagnostic review — multiple derived metrics against one source image. Live: Congestion score →

docs.title: 5. Color foveation demo — Interactive captured to Raster
docs.text: Tools: a live WebGL demo (external) for the interactive itself · muriel/capture.py (capture_responsive() with retina scale factor) · Pillow (crop + composite for editorial placement) · muriel/contrast.py (audit for annotations). Channel: channels/interactive.md captured into channels/raster.md. Pattern: the live version stays interactive; the raster snapshot goes into social cards + paper figures. Live: Color search →

docs.title: 6. Icon analysis pair — Raster + SVG
docs.text: Tools: Pillow (thumbnail resize + compositing) · a Gaussian-blur variant (Pillow's ImageFilter.GaussianBlur) · muriel/typeset.py (label typography) · SVG (hand-rolled or svgwrite) for accompanying diagrams in the post. Channels: channels/raster.md + channels/svg.md. Pattern: micro-comparison at icon scale — two ~256-px tiles laid out inline in editorial prose. When a full figure is overkill.

docs.title: 7. V1 orientation columns — Diagrams + SVG (runnable)
docs.text: Tools: pure Python stdlib (math) emitting SVG directly — a multi-pinwheel orientation field over a hex grid, hand-rolled <line> + <circle> elements with brand tokens inlined from examples/muriel-brand.toml (OLED palette, 8:1+ contrast on every text element). Channels: channels/diagrams.md + channels/svg.md, with channels/science.md sensibility (cited primary literature in the footer). Pattern: deterministic SVG diagram replacing an AI-generated raster — every stroke is a function of position, the topology is reproducible, the file diff-able. Pinwheel singularities marked; one is annotated as a worked-example legend. Run: python examples/gallery/v1-orientation-columns-demo.py → writes docs/v1-orientation-columns.svg. Why it's here: the deterministic-SVG ethos in one file. Scientific basis: Hubel & Wiesel (1962) orientation selectivity; Bonhoeffer & Grinvald (Nature 1991) pinwheel topology.

docs.title: 8. Warm editorial web page — Web
docs.text: Tools: marginalia (editorial CSS library, external) · marginalia-md.js (markdown → marginalia HTML in the browser) · a Node build script · custom CSS for the F-explainer's light palette extensions (.outer-note, .stats-detail, .has-dropcap) · muriel/matplotlibrc_light.py (for any inline figures to match the warm editorial palette). Channel: channels/web.md — marginalia + warm editorial light palette. Pattern: long-form explainer with pull-quotes, margin notes, inline stats spans, drop-cap. Live: Attentional Foraging F-pattern explainer → Note: live and in active use; some supplementary sections are still in draft. Replace this placeholder thumbnail with a real screenshot of the page hero.

docs.title: Refreshing thumbnails
docs.text:
All thumbnails live in thumbs/. Resized to 800px wide max and re-encoded as JPG (85% quality) for files above ~500 KB. If a blog post updates its hero image, re-run:

sips -Z 800 -s format jpeg -s formatOptions 85 source.png --out thumbs/source.jpg

docs.title: Upcoming
docs.text: The dual-brand runnable demo (same brief, two TOMLs, two PNGs side-by-side, exercising muriel.styleguide end-to-end) is the missing piece. Unblocked by the two-tier alias schema; scheduled for 0.6.0.

docs.title: Wavefield proofs
docs.text:
Three deliberately different uses of muriel.patterns.wavefield():

  • decorative-divider.svg uses seeded harmonic synthesis. It carries mood and structure only; it must not be described as data.
  • semantic-signal.svg maps one caller-supplied normalized series exactly. Its accessible description marks the values as illustrative.
  • uncertainty-slices.svg maps five caller-supplied series on one shared normalized scale. They are scenario slices, not a confidence interval.

Regenerate all three from the repository root:

python3 plugins/muriel/skills/compose/examples/wavefield/generate.py

The primitive is a clean-room Muriel implementation. The idea of making layered SVG waves approachable was inspired by anup-a/svgwave; no source code from that project is copied or bundled.

docs.title: Annular interfaces — polar meaning before sci-fi chrome
docs.text:
Use this competency when concentric rings, sectors, spokes, or a central subject carry an interface's actual information or interaction. Annular interface is Muriel's working umbrella, not a claim that the industry has one settled name for every circular screen.

The familiar terms name narrower things:

  • a pie, ring, or radial menu uses direction to select a command;
  • a polar plot or plan-position instrument uses angle and radius as data axes;
  • a dial or annular gauge maps progress or a bounded value to arc length;
  • a cyclic timeline maps phase or time around a period;
  • a sunburst maps hierarchy depth to radius and sibling weight to angle;
  • a reticle establishes a subject, tolerance, or aiming relationship around a centre and may not be interactive at all.

The Science Fiction & Fantasy Stack Exchange discussion calls its examples ring or radial menus. That is accurate only when the sectors are commands. FUI screens often combine several of the other structures in one frame. Classify each ring by what it means before borrowing the silhouette.

docs.title: Use gate
docs.text:
Choose an annular composition when at least one polar relationship is native to the task:

  • direction, bearing, orientation, or phase is primary;
  • distance from a subject matters;
  • the domain is genuinely cyclic;
  • a centre-and-periphery relationship is part of the mental model; or
  • recursive containment benefits from a radial overview.

Prefer a Cartesian chart, table, linear timeline, list, or conventional control when order and comparison are linear, exact cross-item comparison dominates, the centre has no stable meaning, or the circle would merely decorate unrelated readouts. A sci-fi register does not make polar geometry truthful.

docs.title: Start with a semantic declaration
docs.text:
Before drawing, write down the meaning of angle, radius, rings, centre, and motion. A compact host-owned model is enough:

const polarContract = {
  angle: {
    meaning: 'bearing',
    domain: [0, 360],
    zero: 'north',
    direction: 'clockwise',
    unit: 'degrees',
  },
  radius: {
    meaning: 'range',
    domain: [0, 100],
    unit: 'km',
  },
  center: { meaning: 'sensor origin' },
  rings: [
    { id: 'range-gates', role: 'axis', source: 'range scale', update: 'static' },
    { id: 'contacts', role: 'data', source: 'canonical tracks', update: 'event' },
    { id: 'sweep', role: 'feedback', source: 'scan phase', update: 'animation' },
  ],
}

The product owns the values and effects. The annular renderer accepts the contract and projects it into paths, labels, hit regions, and a linear alternative. It does not infer meaning from color, visual proximity, or a clockwise animation.

docs.title: Shared geometry contract
docs.text:
• Use one polar transform and one annular-sector primitive. Data marks, interaction targets, rails, focus paint, and export paths derive from them.
  • Keep semantic geometry immutable across hover, focus, selection, alarm, and live-state changes. Emphasis changes paint, stroke, a halo, or an interior rail; the point, sector, angle, and radius stay put.
  • Separate the data path, paint path, and hit path. A generous target may surround a precise contact or thin arc without changing what the mark means.
  • Declare the angular zero, direction, radial domain, clamping behavior, and whether the centre is data-bearing or a dead zone.
  • Reserve foreground lanes for labels and callouts before adding ornamental rings. A ring that exists only to fill space loses to readable evidence.
  • Measure the rendered result in screen coordinates. Perspective, SVG viewBox scaling, and responsive layout can invalidate clearance that passed in world coordinates.

docs.title: Signal, context, and decoration
docs.text:
Every visible layer belongs to exactly one tier:

  1. Signal — the subject, selected value, alarm, command, or comparison the user is here to read or act on.
  2. Context — axes, range gates, history, uncertainty, thresholds, or provenance needed to interpret the signal.
  3. Decoration — texture or authored atmosphere with no claimed data or control meaning.

Signal and context require a named source, unit when applicable, update rule, and accessible equivalent. Decoration is aria-hidden, pointer-inert, and may not resemble an enabled control. Never promote decoration into context with a plausible-looking number.

Use this admission order when the circle becomes crowded:

  1. selected subject and consequence;
  2. axis meaning, units, and current value;
  3. data marks and uncertainty;
  4. thresholds, history, and comparison guides;
  5. ornament.

docs.title: Centre
docs.text: The centre establishes the frame: sensor origin, current object, pivot, cycle state, or menu hub. Give it one dominant meaning. If the centre alternates between summary, button, label, and decoration without an explicit mode change, the surrounding rings lose their reference.

docs.title: Angle
docs.text: Angle may encode a categorical direction, a measured bearing, hierarchy share, or cyclic time. Do not mix those meanings on one rail. When two angular systems must coexist, distinguish them with separate scales and explicit labels rather than relying on color alone.

docs.title: Radius
docs.text: Radius may encode range, depth, lane, magnitude, or interaction distance. Area grows quadratically, so a radial extent is not automatically a perceptually honest magnitude. For exact comparison, show the number and provide a linear view; for area-proportional partitions, compute area rather than only radius.

docs.title: Rings and sectors
docs.text: Give each ring one job. Sibling rings may share a scale, but a ring should not be simultaneously an axis, progress indicator, menu, and alarm. A sector that can be clicked has an action, state, accessible name, and stable target. A sector that only depicts a zone is pointer-inert.

docs.title: Typography and callouts
docs.text:
• Keep decision text screen-upright by default. Arc-follow labels are suitable for short group names, scale captions, or an explicit tested probe—not for exact values or sentences.
  • Give every important number its label and unit: Bearing 042°, Range 63 km, Cycle 18%. A bare 042 is set dressing.
  • Preserve one physical type floor across responsive states. If SVG scaling would make embedded labels smaller than 16 px, hide those labels and expose a 16 px or larger HTML summary rather than pretending they remain readable.
  • Anchor callouts to real data marks and keep their leader lines pointer-inert. The callout may leave the circle; its target geometry may not move to make room.
  • Keep complete source copy in the semantic tree even when a shorter visible label protects the ring.

Load radial-menus.md when commands must share a wedge with labels, glyphs, status, or exact values. Its rail order and Pretext compositor are stricter than a general instrument needs.

docs.title: Motion has an owner
docs.text:
FUI motion should explain state, not certify futurism.

  • A sweep belongs to sampling phase or search progress.
  • A rotating bearing rail belongs to orientation or a selected frame.
  • A pulse belongs to a new sample, alarm, or confidence change.
  • A trail belongs to history and must declare its time window.
  • A reveal belongs to mode entry or evidence arrival.

Do not rotate several rings at unrelated speeds unless each has an independent, readable variable. Keep targets stable while feedback moves. Pause, reduced motion, background-tab throttling, and deterministic capture must preserve the current values and selection.

docs.title: Input and accessibility
docs.text:
• Pointer hover may preview a mark; click or tap pins it. Pointer exit restores the pinned selection rather than clearing the user's context.
  • Give one predictable keyboard entry to the instrument. Map keys to declared semantics: Left/Right may step by bearing, Home/End by range extrema, and Enter may pin. Do not copy radial-menu depth navigation into a sensor display unless Up/Down genuinely means hierarchy or radius.
  • Provide a linear list or table over the same canonical records. It is both an accessible representation and the responsive fallback—not a second dataset.
  • Make touch targets at least 44 × 44 physical px. When the scaled circle cannot hold them, make the linear surface primary and the circle illustrative.
  • Announce selected identity, state, labeled values, and consequence. Do not narrate decorative ticks or every animation frame.

docs.title: Case 1 — radial command selector
docs.text: Angle is a discrete command. Radius is normally dead-zone plus acquisition distance, but may explicitly become submenu depth or a continuous argument. The important measurements are acquisition time, wrong-wedge entries, label fit, target stability, and one activation per input. The complete contract and runnable comparison live in radial-menus.md and radial-menu-pretext.html.

docs.title: Case 2 — FUI sensor-fusion instrument
docs.text:
Angle is bearing, radius is range, the centre is the simulated sensor origin, and each contact is one canonical record. Range gates are context. The scan sweep is sampling feedback. Confidence changes the contact glyph's interior mark, not its coordinates or target. The selected contact is mirrored into a linear inspector and contact list.

annular-fui-console.html is the runnable second case. It uses deterministic simulated telemetry, declares both polar axes on the surface, supports pointer preview and pinning plus keyboard bearing steps, freezes under reduced motion, and exposes a local audit object for path stability, target size, semantics, and responsive fallback checks.

This case borrows the FUI register without becoming a radial menu. The user does not choose a wedge; they inspect a spatial measurement.

docs.title: Renderer choice
docs.text:
• SVG for polar axes, annular sectors, contact marks, and stable hit paths. It keeps geometry inspectable and scales cleanly.
  • HTML for inspectors, controls, exact values, and the linear equivalent. It preserves ordinary focus, responsive layout, and readable type.
  • Canvas2D for dense trails, sweeps, or waveforms that redraw every frame. Keep semantic targets in DOM/SVG rather than rebuilding accessibility in a bitmap.
  • WebGL/Three.js only when depth, particles, or projection is part of the information contract. A circle does not by itself earn a GPU.

docs.title: Verification matrix
docs.text: Dimension Minimum proof Semantics angle, radius, centre, ring roles, units, and update owners declared Geometry one polar transform; data and target positions stable across state Data truth real source named, or deterministic synthetic data labeled as simulated Density sparse, expected, and worst-case records; overlap and occlusion checked Type every readable line at least 16 physical px; exact values labeled Targets every action at least 40 × 40 px; prefer 44 × 44 for touch Input pointer preview/pin, keyboard semantic steps, touch path, recovery State default, preview, pinned, warning, unavailable, paused, reduced motion Responsive desktop instrument plus linear phone fallback over the same records Motion each moving layer has an owner; pause and deterministic capture work Contrast text at least 8:1; decorative dark-screen strokes at least 55/255 Behavior no duplicate commits, no state inferred from animation or proximity

docs.title: Stop conditions
docs.text:
Fall back to a linear or Cartesian surface when:

  • the angle or centre cannot be named without inventing a metaphor;
  • users need precise comparison across many radial lengths or areas;
  • label fit depends on sub-16 px text or routine mental rotation;
  • interactive marks cannot keep 44 px targets without overlapping neighbors;
  • several rings change independently but their update ownership cannot be explained;
  • the linear equivalent is consistently clearer and the circle adds no spatial task advantage.

Do not add rings, scan lines, random counters, or orbiting particles to rescue an unresolved information model.

docs.title: Lineage
docs.text:
• Don Hopkins's Pie Menu Cookbook defines the directional-command case and distinguishes angle from distance.
  • Microsoft's Surface Dial interaction guidance documents a real radial controller whose menu, rotation, click, context, and occlusion have distinct semantics.
  • In a conversation about film interfaces, Jayse Hansen describes researching the real information a character would need; the useful lesson is that circles and random text do not substitute for an information model.

docs.title: Collections — an explorer for many images
docs.text:
Use this reference when the deliverable is a set of images that a person will survey, filter, compare or check, rather than one composed figure. muriel's default engine for this is Wunderkammer 0.3.0 (MIT), a collection explorer for people and language models:

  • The agent writes the collection as one JSON document.
  • The person pans, zooms, filters by facets, groups, compares groups and opens items.
  • The agent reads back exactly what the person selected.

It runs from static files with no server.

Wunderkammer's spatial view uses muriel's rendering primitives, vendored at a pinned commit (wall/spatial/lib/VENDOR.md). muriel imports no Wunderkammer code, and this reference names it by released version only. Every URL below is pinned to the v0.3.0 tag, the agent skill included. When a new version is released, update the pins and re-check the claims that carry a date.

This reference is the front door. Wunderkammer is designed to be used from muriel: this reference decides when an explorer is the right representation, muriel.collection builds the document, and the exploration-quality axis and contrast checks review the result. For the engine's own steps and traps (URL keys, hosting, observations, the hand-back), read Wunderkammer's skill, skills/wunderkammer/SKILL.md. Its examples are tested against the pages' validators, so where it or the contract disagrees with the summary below, they win. Agents without muriel can install that skill on its own (npx skills add andyed/wunderkammer).

It is a default, not a requirement. Another explorer that passes the exploration-quality axis is a sensible substitute: the axis is muriel's opinion, and the engine is a preference.

docs.title: When to reach for a collection explorer
docs.text:
Use one when at least one of these holds:

  • Dozens to thousands of images. Below a dozen, a figure grid or contact sheet is faster to read than an explorer is to learn. Above that, a person needs an overview, filters and a way back to where they were. A document can list 1 to 50,000 items. The bundled example has 297.
  • A comparison between groups. The question is how an attribute is distributed across 2–6 groups (decades, sources, conditions), and the person should see the items in each group, not only their shares. If the images are irrelevant to the question, use channels/charts.md.
  • Claims a person should be able to check. The agent says something about the collection, such as "jazz is less common in the 1990s", and the person should be able to open the exact items behind it.

Do not use one for a single image or composed figure, or for numbers with no images behind them. When the output must be one self-contained file, see the fallback.

An arrival, or a video. ?view=warehouse (since 0.3.0; also asked for as the "matrix guns view") opens the wall's aisle with "Cats. Lots of cats." played over it once. Rows of racks rush out of a white void, and then the lights go down on the aisle, ready to browse. The word in the caption is the document's ui.nouns.items. Wunderkammer's scripts/warehouse-video.mjs renders the same frames to an MP4; --tour 30 ends it with half a minute panning over every cover. See its AISLE.md.

From Apple Photos. On a Mac, Wunderkammer's scripts/photos-collection.py builds the document from the Photos library, read-only, through osxphotos. It finds one subject (a pet, a person, a trip) by Photos' labels, captions or named people and pets, then keeps a tidy 150: one per burst, spread over time, and with --animal dog, only photos where the dog can be seen. Its images carry no location. It is macOS-only, so it lives in the engine, not in muriel.collection; see APPLE_PHOTOS.md.

docs.title: The contract in brief
docs.text: There are four parts, and all of them are static files. The full contract is docs/CONTRACT.md. This section summarizes it for design decisions; for the engine's steps, see Wunderkammer's skill above.

docs.title: Collection document: wunderkammer.collection v1
docs.text:
{
  "format": "wunderkammer.collection",
  "version": 1,
  "corpus": { "id": "example:album-covers", "revision": "2026-10-17" },
  "ui": { "title": "Album covers", "defaultGroup": "decade",
          "facetOrder": ["decade", "genre"], "hiddenFacets": ["catalog"] },
  "images": { "cors": true },
  "clips": [
    { "id": "a1", "title": "Example title",
      "cover": "https://example.org/a1-256.webp",
      "props": { "decade": "1980s", "genre": ["electronic", "pop"], "catalog": "XL-104" },
      "sourceUrl": "https://example.org/a1" }
  ]
}
  • Required fields: format, version, corpus.id and clips (1 to 50,000 items). Each clip needs a non-empty id.
  • Identity: an item's identity is its url, or its id when it has no url. Repeated identities are an error.
  • Attributes go in props as strings, finite numbers, booleans or arrays of them. Facets and their counts are derived from props, so supply neither yourself. Hide per-item identifiers with ui.hiddenFacets. A props key that names a clip field (title, source …) is refused.
  • Links and images: sourceUrl must be http(s). Images (cover, detailCover, coverVariants[].src, media[].src) may be http(s), data:image/ or blob:. Relative URLs resolve against the document's URL.
  • Cross-origin covers: images.cors: true declares that covers on other origins send CORS headers. Without CORS, those covers stay blank in the 3D views.
  • Plain text only: every string is set as text (textContent). note is never HTML.
  • Validation: unknown keys are refused, with the list of supported ones. All problems are reported at once with their paths, up to 25 in one CollectionError, so a first draft can be fixed in a single pass.
  • Sprite sheets: with a few hundred covers or more, pack them into sprite-sheet pages with scripts/collection-sheets.py. On the 297-image example, the overview needed 3 image requests instead of 297 (docs/PERF.md, "Collection sprite sheets").

docs.title: Comparison recipe
docs.text:
A question-sized comparison: 2–6 groups of one attribute, one measured attribute, and counts or shares. Every field is required, though question and scope.query may be empty strings.

{
  "version": 1,
  "question": "How does genre distribution change across release decades?",
  "corpus": { "id": "example:album-covers", "revision": "2026-10-17" },
  "scope": { "query": "", "facets": {} },
  "groupBy": "decade", "groups": ["1970s", "1980s", "1990s"],
  "measure": "genre", "metric": "share",
  "categoryLimit": 8, "sort": "difference"
}
  • Allowed values:
  • metric: share or count;
  • sort: difference, total or name;
  • categoryLimit: an integer from 4 to 20.
  • Corpus: repeat the collection's corpus.id and corpus.revision. Otherwise the page notes that the recipe names a different corpus.
  • Validation: validateComparison() stops at the first problem, unlike the collection and observation validators.
  • Counting: the rules are stated in the evidence packet's countingPolicy:
  • an item can fall in several groups and carry several values, so shares need not sum to one;
  • an absent attribute counts as (Unknown);
  • a share with a zero denominator is null.

docs.title: Observations: wunderkammer.observations v1
docs.text:
An observation is a claim about a comparison. It points at the cells or items behind it rather than summarizing them.

{
  "format": "wunderkammer.observations", "version": 1,
  "comparison": { "version": 1, "...": "the recipe above, unchanged" },
  "observations": [
    { "id": "jazz-falls",
      "text": "Jazz is less common in the 1990s than in the 1970s.",
      "evidence": { "cells": [{ "value": "Jazz", "cohort": "1970s" },
                              { "value": "Jazz", "cohort": "1990s" }],
                    "items": ["a1"] } }
  ]
}
  • The figures are computed by the page. Each cited cell's count, denominator and share are taken from the same rows as the evidence export. In the panel, the text is labelled as the author's and the figures as computed. v1 does not parse numbers out of the text, so an authored claim has no numbers of its own. State the direction and cite the cells. The size is then shown by the page.
  • Limits:
  • 12 observations;
  • 600 characters of text, 12 cells and 200 items per observation;
  • ids of 1–40 letters, digits, - or _.
  • Cells: a cell's cohort must be one of the recipe's groups. A cell without one cites its value in every group.
  • Unresolved citations are shown, never dropped. These are a value the measure lacks, a group the recipe lacks, or an item outside the collection.
  • Staleness: observations apply to the comparison they were written for. After the person changes it, they are shown without figures, with a button back to the original comparison.
  • Delivery: two static files, wall/compare.html?collection=<collection.json>&observations=<observations.json>. Once loaded, the observations travel in the page's link.

docs.title: Hand-back: window.wunderkammer.export()
docs.text:
Both pages define window.wunderkammer.export(). Only identities and titles are in the packet, never notes or paths.

  • The wall returns { format: "wunderkammer.export", version: 1, … }:
  • corpus;
  • scope: label, query, facets and branch counts;
  • view: mode and grouping;
  • focus: the focused item;
  • highlight: the pinned highlight with its matching keys;
  • count and total;
  • evidence: every in-scope item as { key, title }, in corpus order.
  • The comparison page returns the evidence packet for the current selection:
  • cohorts with their denominators;
  • rows of cells with count, share and keys;
  • countingPolicy, coverage and warnings;
  • the selected items.

For a selected observation, the packet adds observation, with its computed figures and any unresolved citations. - Reading it: open the page as the top-level document in a browser the agent drives, and evaluate window.wunderkammer.export() with the page-JavaScript tool. In the Claude Code desktop app, that is the browser pane's javascript_tool. - Frames: a same-origin frame can be read as frame.contentWindow.wunderkammer.export(), but a cross-origin frame cannot. - Not built in 0.3.0: an onSelection callback through mount(), and a "copy for the conversation" button. - Before acting on a packet, check that its count matches the scope the person described. Quote identities from the packet rather than from memory of the page.

docs.title: Embedding: mount(element, collection)
docs.text:
// A checkout of v0.3.0, served by the same static host as this page.
import { mount } from './wunderkammer/wall/embed.mjs';

const wall = mount(element, collection);   // frames ./wunderkammer/index.html
await wall.ready;                          // resolves on the wall's view-ready message
  • collection is an object or a URL.
  • An object is validated in the host page first, so a bad one throws a CollectionError before any frame exists. It is then posted to the wall's origin only, and validated again there.
  • A URL is fetched by the wall. If it fails, the host gets a generic error and the details appear inside the frame.
  • wallUrl defaults to the wall page, index.html at the checkout's root, one folder above embed.mjs. Imported from a static host, the default works as it is. The module can also be imported from jsDelivr's GitHub route, https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/andyed/wunderkammer@v0.3.0/wall/embed.mjs, but its default is then a page served as text/plain. Pass mount(element, collection, { wallUrl }) with a static host's wall page.
  • Other options: title (the iframe's title) and timeout (default 20,000 ms).
  • wall.ready rejects on the wall's error message or on timeout. wall.destroy() removes the frame.

docs.title: Loading by pinned version
docs.text:
Wunderkammer is released as git tags on GitHub. Pin every reference to the tag, v0.3.0: in a GitHub URL, in a jsDelivr GitHub-route URL, and as the checkout a static host serves. Never use a branch, @latest, or a package-registry URL. No Wunderkammer package is published, so such a URL fails today, and would serve someone else's code if they registered the name.

What jsDelivr GitHub route (cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/andyed/wunderkammer@v0.3.0/…) Static host serving a checkout of the tag ES modules (wall/embed.mjs, wall/collection.mjs, wall/observations.mjs) yes yes The wall (index.html) and wall/compare.html, opened or framed no: HTML is served as text/plain yes
  • Content types were checked on 2026-10-18 on the GitHub route at v0.1.0: index.html and wall/compare.html are served as text/plain, and wall/embed.mjs as application/javascript.
  • Where the pages are. The wall is index.html at the checkout's root, with its assets under wall/: <host>/<path>/index.html?collection=<url>. The comparison page is wall/compare.html. Both name their assets by relative paths, so they work at any sub-path, such as a GitHub Pages project site. tests/cdn-subpath.test.mjs serves the release's files under a versioned sub-path. From there it boots the wall, mount() with its default, and the comparison page's link back, with no request leaving that path.
  • A static host: a checkout of the tag (git clone --branch v0.3.0 https://github.com/andyed/wunderkammer, then npx http-server -p 8080 . and /?collection=<url>), the output of scripts/build-demo.mjs, or a wunderkammer server. All of them serve the wall at /.
  • To try a document without hosting the wall, open the live demo with ?collection=<url>, which takes precedence over the demo's own collection. The document must be served with CORS. The demo is not pinned to a tag, so validate for the pinned release anyway.
  • Framing from an artifact host is untested. The live demo sends no X-Frame-Options or frame-ancestors header (checked 2026-10-18), so framing it is governed by the host page's own content security policy. A static host of your own sets its own headers.
  • Three.js 0.186.1 is loaded from jsDelivr by both pages, for the 3D views (the spatial view, the aisle and the floating space) and the album walls only. Without the network or WebGL, those views are withdrawn with a notice. The flat wall, facets, detail pane, comparison matrix and evidence list remain usable.

docs.title: Fallback
docs.text:
Use muriel's linked-atlas lab instead of Wunderkammer when:

  • A single file is required. Wunderkammer is a wall page, its modules and a collection document, with Three.js from a CDN, and it cannot be inlined into one HTML file. The lab has no runtime dependencies: one page, one stylesheet and three small ES modules, all of which can be inlined.
  • WebGL is unavailable and the task needs the views that use it. Wunderkammer's 3D view and album walls need WebGL. Its flat wall and comparison matrix do not, so check which views the task needs before switching.

The lab is drawn in SVG and HTML, and includes:

  • semantic zoom with hysteresis, and an overview linked to a detail view;
  • brushing with replace, add, subtract and intersect;
  • summaries that show selected/total denominators;
  • an accessible record table;
  • undo;
  • a read-only window.linkedAtlas.snapshot().

It is a reference implementation of the interaction contract for 192 synthetic records, not a collection engine. It has no image tiles, document validator, comparison recipe or observations. Adopting it means writing those against its model while keeping its selection and camera semantics.

docs.title: Exploration quality
docs.text:
This is a critique axis for any collection page, whether Wunderkammer or a substitute. Each question is answered from evidence an agent can gather:

  • a screenshot at fit-to-all;
  • one after zooming into a group;
  • one after opening and closing an item;
  • the hand-back packet.

Report each failure with its evidence, in muriel-critique's severity scale.

Question Passes when Evidence Severity if it fails Does the overview show the collection's structure? At fit-to-all, every item is on screen, grouped by an attribute that answers the person's first question, each group is labelled with its count, and the total is shown. Fit-to-all screenshot, and export().total against the document's item count. HIGH: for example, an ungrouped grid, or grouping by a per-item attribute such as a file name. Are the facets useful, with counts? Each visible facet splits the collection into two or more values, none of which covers nearly every item. Every value shows its count, with the count's meaning named (Wunderkammer: In view / available). Facets have readable labels (ui.facetLabels), and per-item identifiers are hidden. Facet-rail screenshot. For each props key, the number of distinct values against the number of items. MEDIUM. HIGH when counts are missing. Does zoom keep orientation? After zooming into a group, the group's name is still visible. The whole collection is one action away (Fit or Back). Opening and closing an item returns to the same view. A zoom limit is a no-op, not a jump. Before and after screenshots, and export().scope and export().view before and after opening an item. HIGH. Can a selection be handed back? The person's scope, focus and selection can be read as exact identities, the packet's count equals the count on screen, and the packet holds no notes or local paths. The hand-back packet against the on-screen count. HIGH when there is no packet or the counts disagree. CRITICAL when private fields leak. Do observations cite evidence? Every observation cites at least one cell or item, and none is unresolved. The text contains no figures of its own. Selecting an observation lights exactly its cited items. Observation panel, and the packet's observation.figures and observation.unresolved. CRITICAL when an authored number disagrees with the computed figure. HIGH for an observation with nothing resolvable.

The universal rules still apply. Facet labels, counts, group titles and observation text are readable text under the 8:1 floor:

  • Wunderkammer's own audit: its facet and scope controls measured at least 8.528:1 against their painted backgrounds (docs/FACETING.md). That audit did not cover every text element.
  • The embedding page: run python -m muriel.contrast <page.html> on the page you wrote.
  • The rest of the wall's text: measure it on a capture (python -m muriel.capture <url>).

docs.title: Building a document: muriel.collection
docs.text:
python -m muriel.collection build <folder|csv> --out collection.json [--title T] [--group FIELD]
python -m muriel.collection validate collection.json [--release 0.1.0|next]
  • build reads a folder of images or a CSV and writes a wunderkammer.collection v1 document. --title names the collection, and --group names the attribute the wall groups by when it opens.
  • validate follows muriel's CLI convention for exit codes:
  • exit 0: the document is valid;
  • exit 1: every problem is listed with its path;
  • exit 2: nothing was read.
  • Validate before opening a browser. A collection given to a frame by URL reports its problems inside the frame, not to the host. The page validates again on load, and when the two validators disagree, the page's (wall/collection.mjs) is the reference.
  • --release names the wall that will load the document. Each release refuses the fields added after it. The default is 0.3.0, the release this reference pins; it adds no collection fields, so a document valid for 0.2.0 loads in it. For a 0.1.0 wall, validate with --release 0.1.0: it refuses ui.nouns (what the counts call one item and several), which 0.2.0 added. --release next checks for Wunderkammer's unreleased work after 0.3.0, which adds a clip's video: one http(s) or blob: URL, never data:, played muted and looping over the clip's cover in the 3D views and the aisle, and with controls in the detail pane. A 0.3.0 wall refuses it, so the default check refuses it too.
  • Observations need Wunderkammer's checker. muriel.collection validates the collection document only. From a Wunderkammer checkout, node scripts/validate-collection.mjs collection.json --observations observations.json also prints the figures each claim will show and every citation that does not resolve.

A typical pass:

  1. Build and validate the document, then fix every listed problem.
  2. Open the wall (index.html) with ?collection= and check the overview against the exploration-quality axis.
  3. For a comparison, write the recipe. For claims, write observations that cite cells. Open wall/compare.html with both.
  4. Let the person explore, then read the hand-back and quote the identities in it.

docs.title: Anti-patterns
docs.text:
• Numbers in observation text. Cite the cell, and let the page show the figure.
  • A summary in place of the collection. Show the collection, and use observations as pointers into it.
  • @latest, a branch URL, a package-registry URL, or the wall page from jsDelivr. Pin the tag, and serve HTML from a static host.
  • HTML in note or title. It is shown as literal text.
  • Treating the hand-back as the person's conclusion. It records what they selected, not what they concluded from it.

docs.title: Creative provocations — invention and controlled disturbance
docs.text:
Use this reference as an optional divergent pass inside design synthesis. It is inspired by the role of Brian Eno and Peter Schmidt's Oblique Strategies: introduce a well-timed constraint or reframing that interrupts a locally coherent answer. This is an original transformation set, not a reproduction of their card text.

Use it for deliberate invention as well as escaping a rut. A familiar convention may be worth challenging while it still works; explore what a different mechanism could make possible, then shape a tangible probe.

A provocation is not a decision framework and does not outrank product truth. Its job is to expose an assumption, produce a materially different mechanism, and then submit that mechanism to evidence, constraints, and integration.

docs.title: Contents
docs.text:
1. Activation gate
  2. Fit the disturbance
  3. Transformation repertoire
  4. Run the pass
  5. Return to truth
  6. Observable record
  7. Anti-patterns
  8. Sources and adaptation

docs.title: Activation gate
docs.text:
Use a provocation when at least one is true:

  • all current options preserve the same state, sequence, actor, boundary, or feedback assumption;
  • the work is producing cosmetic variants instead of different mechanisms;
  • expertise is narrowing the space before the risky premise has been tested;
  • a Compare or Probe is stuck and needs a new discriminating move;
  • the user explicitly asks for brainstorming or an oblique angle.
  • an unsettled direction calls for inventing an interaction or deliberately departing from convention.

Skip it when the desired behavior is settled, the task is a local correctness or accessibility fix, an urgent incident needs stabilization, or novelty would only delay an obvious safe action.

Use one fitted transformation first. Use two or three only when the user wants breadth or the first one fails to perturb the mechanism. Never dump the whole repertoire into the answer.

docs.title: Fit the disturbance
docs.text:
Diagnose the kind of sameness before choosing a transformation:

Sameness in the option set Start with Every option adds another surface, control, or explanation Subtract, merge roles, background it Every option preserves the same sequence or cadence Reverse sequence, delay, change rhythm Every option gives agency to the same actor Transfer agency, change witness Every option treats failure as interruption or loss Make residue useful, turn failure into evidence Every option lives at the same scale Zoom in, zoom out, change the unit Every option assumes one boundary or category Move the boundary, split the bundle Every option optimizes the same goal Replace the score, protect the anomaly The idea is abstract and hard to feel Translate medium, make state tangible

Prefer a transformation that attacks the suspected assumption. When no assumption is visible, select from different families rather than drawing several near-duplicates.

docs.title: Transformation repertoire
docs.text: The labels below are stable ids for observability. The questions are generative, not requirements.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
• PV-S1 — Subtract the apparatus. If one layer, modal, dashboard, control, or explanation disappeared, what would the underlying experience need to reveal by itself?
  • PV-S2 — Split the bundle. Which supposedly single event contains two institutions, motives, time scales, or consequences that should diverge?
  • PV-S3 — Merge the roles. What happens if two components, actors, or states become one mechanism with two readings?
  • PV-S4 — Move the boundary. If the feature began one step earlier or ended one step later, where would the meaningful decision move?

docs.title: Sequence and time
docs.text:
• PV-T1 — Reverse cause and reveal. Let the consequence or evidence arrive before the explanation. What becomes suspense, strategy, or comprehension?
  • PV-T2 — Change the rhythm. Replace a single dramatic interruption with an accumulation, deadline, decay, recurring ritual, or slow recovery.
  • PV-T3 — Design the echo. What residue should a choice leave several turns, screens, or sessions later so that it becomes part of the system's memory?
  • PV-T4 — Borrow from the next era. Which future pressure can appear now in a small, historically or product-truthful form without implementing the future system?

docs.title: Agency and viewpoint
docs.text:
• PV-A1 — Transfer agency. Give the consequential action to the least obvious legitimate actor: the user, customer, rival, system, regulator, environment, or future self.
  • PV-A2 — Change the witness. How would the same state read to someone who does not control it but must interpret, trust, recover from, or audit it?
  • PV-A3 — Make self-exposure strategic. What if progress requires the actor to create, disclose, certify, or preserve evidence that can later constrain them?
  • PV-A4 — Let the system refuse. Where would a legible refusal, delay, or counter-offer create more agency than another available action?

docs.title: Scale and medium
docs.text:
• PV-M1 — Change the unit. Reframe the experience around a batch, receipt, relationship, route, promise, or season instead of the current unit.
  • PV-M2 — Translate the medium. If the state had to be understood as a timeline, map, ledger, conversation, physical object, or ambient signal, which relation would become visible?
  • PV-M3 — Zoom to the seam. What happens at the handoff between two states, actors, or institutions, and could that seam become the primary interaction?
  • PV-M4 — Zoom to the system. Which local action is actually a feedback loop, network effect, legitimacy shift, or accumulating debt when seen over time?

docs.title: Value, error, and constraint
docs.text:
• PV-V1 — Preserve the anomaly. Which awkward exception contains product or domain truth that a clean solution is erasing?
  • PV-V2 — Make failure informative. Instead of repeating punishment, what new state, evidence, leverage, or recovery route can failure create?
  • PV-V3 — Swap the scarce resource. If money, time, attention, trust, legitimacy, information, or reversibility became the binding constraint, how would the mechanism change?
  • PV-V4 — Replace the score. What would the user pursue if the dominant metric disappeared and the underlying value had to become directly legible?

docs.title: Productive contradiction
docs.text:
• PV-C1 — Honor both demands. Treat the apparent tradeoff as a request for a new mechanism: what could make both qualities true without averaging them?
  • PV-C2 — Intensify the constraint. Temporarily make the hardest constraint absolute. Which simpler structure survives?
  • PV-C3 — Design the opposite honestly. Build the strongest version of the rejected direction. What valid need was the favored direction hiding?
  • PV-C4 — Reuse the liability. Which cost, delay, record, or restriction can become feedback, identity, pacing, proof, or future leverage?

docs.title: Run the pass
docs.text:
For each selected transformation:

  1. Name the sameness. State the assumption shared by the current options.
  2. Apply the transformation. Ask the fitted question against the actual artifact and product truth, not in the abstract.
  3. Generate an option delta. Describe the changed state, rule, information flow, interaction, or composition in one or two sentences.
  4. Name the leverage. Identify the immediate value and any independent benefit caused by the same mechanism.
  5. Return to truth. Keep, adapt, or drop the delta using the gate below.

Do not ask the user to pick a cryptic card without context. The agent may show a small hand of two or three fitted provocations when collaborative selection is itself useful, but must explain what each is trying to disturb.

docs.title: Return to truth
docs.text:
A provocative option is eligible for comparison or probing only if it can answer:

  • Truth: Which locked behaviors, facts, safety limits, and authority boundaries does it preserve?
  • Difference: Did it change a mechanism, or only the story told about one?
  • Integration: Which canonical state, rule, component, registry, or production path would carry it?
  • Value: What immediate user-visible benefit appears without waiting for a speculative platform or later era?
  • Cost: What becomes harder, riskier, slower, or less legible?
  • Learning: What rendered state, trace, play session, or safe-to-fail probe can distinguish it from the baseline?

Adapt a useful provocation when its literal version violates a constraint. Drop it when the only defense is novelty, metaphor, or future reuse.

docs.title: Observable record
docs.text:
Add one compact field to the Muriel synthesis for each provocation used:

Provocation: PV-A3 transfer agency
Assumption challenged: enforcement only happens to the player
Option delta: player-generated compliance evidence can later create exposure
Disposition: adapted into the bounded lab-and-recall probe
Signal: players distinguish compliance exposure from a raid and can name recovery

For a durable machine-readable trace, use a versioned event. The record is a decision artifact, not hidden reasoning:

{"kind":"muriel.provocation","version":1,"decision_id":"era4-enforcement","provocation_id":"PV-A3","assumption":"enforcement only happens to the player","delta":"player-generated evidence creates later exposure","disposition":"adapted","evidence_ref":"seeded-era4-lab-trace"}

At minimum record provocation_id, assumption, delta, and disposition. Add an evidence reference when the delta is tested. Use kept, adapted, or dropped; do not imply that use of a prompt makes its result correct.

docs.title: Anti-patterns
docs.text:
• Random ceremony — drawing a prompt when the task already has a clear, evidence-backed answer.
  • Novelty laundering — passing a whimsical metaphor off as product insight.
  • Prompt dumping — showing the repertoire instead of making a decision.
  • Constraint amnesia — letting the provocation erase accessibility, safety, domain truth, canonical ownership, or the user's task boundary.
  • Cosmetic divergence — producing new language or skins around the same trigger, stakes, choice, and recovery.
  • Untraceable inspiration — keeping a surprising answer without naming the challenged assumption or proof.
  • Deck dependence — refusing to explore because a literal card draw, random source, or external tool is unavailable.

docs.title: Sources and adaptation
docs.text:
The mechanism is informed by Oblique Strategies and by open repositories that treat creative prompts as constraints rather than answers. GitHub wrappers are useful implementation examples, but their software licenses do not necessarily grant rights to reproduce third-party card text. Keep Muriel's repertoire original and attribute the conceptual influence.

  • Jake Dahn's oblique-skill demonstrates a small-hand interaction: present a few strategies, select one, and apply it to the current problem.
  • Hermes Agent's creative-ideation skill demonstrates matching a constraint to the domain and producing concrete outputs instead of abstract inspiration.
  • 18F Methods demonstrates a CC0, inspectable method-card library with a shared structure and vocabulary.
  • awesome-claude-design demonstrates independent design voices followed by synthesis and preserved minority views.

Muriel borrows the operational patterns—timed constraint, fitted application, structured record, and preserved disagreement—not protected prompt wording.

docs.title: Design synthesis — choose what earns implementation
docs.text:
Use this reference when the human-visible direction is not settled. Frame the decision, explore materially different mechanisms, find shared leverage, choose with explicit tradeoffs, and shape the smallest useful proof before polishing the surface.

Do not use this reference as a license to own product truth, domain balance, or code architecture. The calling agent retains those responsibilities. Muriel makes the visible design decision coherent, legible, adaptable, and observable.

docs.title: Contents
docs.text:
1. Load gate
  2. Adaptive depth
  3. Synthesis loop
  4. Creative perturbation
  5. Leverage and synergy
  6. Choosing without false precision
  7. Shape the investment
  8. Observable rationale
  9. Proof and anti-patterns

docs.title: Load gate
docs.text:
Load before the primary visual channel when the task asks one or more of:

  • what or why to build before how to render it;
  • how a new feature, mode, gameplay grammar, information architecture, or interaction concept should work;
  • which of several plausible directions deserves implementation;
  • how one investment can create several independent benefits through shared state, rules, information flows, or production paths;
  • how to break an ambiguous direction into a bounded, testable slice;
  • how to preserve useful future choices without building a speculative platform.

Do not load for a local correctness, accessibility, typography, spacing, or surface fix whose desired behavior is already settled. Do not load for backend-only work. A necessary single-reason fix does not need a manufactured strategy narrative.

docs.title: Adaptive depth
docs.text:
Choose the minimum sufficient ceremony. Base depth on uncertainty, reversibility, blast radius, and evidence gaps. Do not average these into a decorative score.

Mode Use when Required output Direct A known pattern fits; impact is local, reversible, and supported by evidence Decision, integration, proof Compare Several defensible answers exist; expertise or cross-cutting tradeoffs matter Question, 2–4 options, criteria, leverage, decision, proof Probe The effect depends on real use or emergent behavior; analysis cannot predict the winner Competing hypotheses or slices, safe-to-fail bounds, signals, expand/stop conditions

State the selected mode and why in the Muriel entry contract. Change modes when new evidence changes the nature of the decision. Do not keep a task in Probe after a pattern has stabilized, or force Compare when one option clearly meets the constraints and the others do not.

Route to Probe when the decisive criterion can only be learned through real use, play, comprehension, or emergent system behavior. The presence of several named options does not make the task Compare; QOC can organize options inside a Probe. Use Compare only when existing evidence and analysis can credibly select the direction.

Treat urgent chaotic incidents as the calling agent's operational problem, not as a Muriel ideation exercise. Stabilize first; synthesize the human-visible recovery later.

docs.title: Synthesis loop
docs.text:
Run only the stages required by the selected mode:

Frame → Route → Explore → [Provoke] → Connect → Choose → Shape → Observe

docs.title: 1. Frame
docs.text:
Record:

  • Outcome — the user or audience change the work should cause.
  • Focal decision — one question whose answer changes implementation.
  • Product truth — locked behavior, domain facts, and authority boundaries.
  • Canonical integration — existing state, component, service, registry, or production path that may carry the choice.
  • Evidence — observed artifact behavior, research, tests, traces, or user input already available.
  • Assumptions — plausible claims not yet established.
  • Unknowns — gaps that could reverse the decision.

When a research-informed mechanism determines the choice, use the selected channel's academic lineage and, when needed, human-capabilities.md. Connect the source or framework to the interaction being built and the evidence that can test it. Carry this into the existing synthesis; keep one decision record.

Keep facts, assumptions, and concepts visibly separate. Do not let a fluent concept silently become project truth.

docs.title: 2. Route
docs.text: Select Direct, Compare, or Probe. Name the factor that set the depth. Prefer a small proof over a long analysis when real use is the only credible source of evidence.

docs.title: 3. Explore
docs.text:
Generate mechanisms, not cosmetic variants. Include a baseline or smallest change when it is viable. Each option must differ in state, rules, information flow, interaction, composition, or user leverage—not merely in naming or skin.

Do not fill an option quota. Two real alternatives are better than four padded ones. Preserve surprising concepts long enough to test their mechanism, but do not protect novelty from product constraints.

Conventions are revisable design choices. Challenge or replace them when a different mechanism opens worthwhile task, expressive, or experiential value. A novel interaction can be a first-class option before a conventional approach has failed. Use research to reason about its mechanism without requiring a published precedent for the exact invention. Where its value depends on use, route to Probe and build enough to test it. Include familiar alternatives when they make the tradeoff informative; assess learning and recovery costs alongside what the invention makes possible.

docs.title: Optional: Provoke
docs.text:
Do not draw a provocation by default. Load creative-provocations.md when:

  • the first options are variations of one hidden assumption;
  • the exploration changes labels, styling, or intensity but not the mechanism;
  • a favored direction has become too coherent to question;
  • a Compare or Probe has stalled without producing a discriminating move; or
  • the user explicitly asks to brainstorm, get unstuck, or seek an oblique angle.

The repertoire can also support deliberate invention early in exploration; there need not be an existing design rut.

Use one fitted transformation first. Use at most three when breadth is the purpose. Record what assumption each challenged and what changed. A provocation earns a place in the option set only after it returns through product truth, constraints, evidence, and canonical integration.

docs.title: 4. Connect
docs.text:
Look for one shared mechanism that creates several benefits. Check canonical state, information flows, feedback loops, rules, and goals before proposing a new abstraction. Ask:

  • What immediate user-visible problem does the investment solve?
  • What existing inconsistency or duplication does the same mechanism remove?
  • What does it make easier to learn, test, explain, or verify?
  • Which named, plausible next use can adopt it without another parallel model?
  • Which future choices remain available without being implemented now?

Then run the leverage and synergy tests below.

docs.title: 5. Choose
docs.text:
Use Questions, Options, and Criteria as a compact design-space record. Mark how each option supports, conflicts with, or remains unknown against each criterion. Add evidence beside the judgment.

Apply hard constraints before tradeoffs. Eliminate an option that violates product truth, accessibility, safety, canonical ownership, or the task boundary; do not let strengths elsewhere compensate for a fatal weakness.

docs.title: 6. Shape
docs.text: Turn the choice into a thin slice with explicit exclusions, integration, and proof. Distinguish enabling work required by the slice from infrastructure that would only benefit hypothetical future work.

docs.title: 7. Observe
docs.text: Emit a public rationale summary at the depth required by the mode. Record evidence, options, assumptions, decisions, and proof—not private chain-of-thought or a chronological transcript of every idea.

docs.title: Leverage and synergy
docs.text:
Use a lightweight leverage ladder:

  1. Parameter or surface — copy, timing, color, number, local layout.
  2. Information or feedback — what becomes visible, when, and to whom.
  3. Rule or canonical state — permissions, transitions, incentives, constraints, ownership.
  4. Goal or mental model — what the system teaches the user to pursue or understand.

Prefer the highest justified intervention, not the highest imaginable one. A surface fix is correct when the underlying model is already right. A new skin is not a new grammar when the same trigger, stakes, choices, and recovery remain.

Call an investment synergistic only when:

  • one named mechanism directly causes at least two benefits;
  • each benefit remains valuable if another disappears;
  • the benefits share implementation, state, rules, or evidence—not merely a release milestone;
  • at least one benefit is immediate;
  • any reuse claim names a plausible near-term consumer;
  • the shared mechanism reduces total complexity or creates justified optionality.

Treat optionality as the right, not the obligation, to take a later action. Do not implement the later action to prove the option exists. Prefer a narrow seam, stable contract, or canonical field over a general platform with no current consumer.

Permit single-reason investments when the reason is sufficient: correctness, accessibility, safety, legal truth, or a locked product requirement does not need reason inflation.

docs.title: Choosing without false precision
docs.text:
Start with qualitative QOC:

Field Required answer Question What decision changes implementation? Options What materially different mechanisms could answer it? Criteria What outcomes, constraints, risks, and evidence distinguish them? Judgment Supports, conflicts, or unknown—with evidence Decision Which option, at what confidence and status?

Common criteria include user value, product truth, strategic anticipation, mechanical or perceptual distinctness, canonical integration, accessibility, cost, risk, reversibility, learning value, and proof quality. Select only criteria that can change the decision.

Do not use default numeric weights. Use a weighted or multi-criteria matrix only when several live options remain after hard constraints, stakeholders genuinely value criteria differently, and the scales can be explained. Treat the result as decision support, not an automatic answer. Run a sensitivity check before trusting a narrow winner.

docs.title: Shape the investment
docs.text:
Write a design thesis:

  • Decision — the mechanism to build or test.
  • Immediate value — the first user-visible outcome.
  • Independent reasons — the other benefits that pass the independence test.
  • Shared leverage — the canonical mechanism producing those benefits.
  • Tradeoffs — what becomes harder, costlier, or less flexible.
  • Thin slice — the smallest complete experience that tests the thesis.
  • Enablers — only the shared work the thin slice actually requires.
  • Excluded — adjacent work deliberately left out.
  • Proof — observable signals, rendered states, exercised paths, or tests.
  • Options preserved — later actions enabled but not implemented.

For Probe mode, define two or more safe-to-fail probes only when they can teach different things. For each probe specify:

  • hypothesis and uncertainty;
  • bounded scope and downside;
  • sensor or observation method;
  • success, stop, and expansion signals;
  • decision the result will inform.

docs.title: Observable rationale
docs.text:
Treat one Muriel consultation as a design trace. Treat Frame, Explore, Choose, and Shape as conceptual spans; treat an assumption change, option rejection, scope change, or proof result as an event; link related earlier decisions; and mark the decision proposed, accepted, proven, or superseded.

When a provocation was used, also record its stable id or transformation family, the assumption it challenged, the option delta it caused, and whether that delta was kept, adapted, or dropped. Do not record a private reasoning transcript.

Always expose a concise human-readable summary. Use only the fields required by the mode:

Muriel synthesis
Decision ID: <stable task-local id when persistence matters>
Mode: direct | compare | probe — <why>
Question: <focal decision>
Evidence: <facts and inspected sources>
Options: <material alternatives; omit in Direct>
Provocation: <id/family → assumption → option delta → disposition; omit if unused>
Criteria: <decision-changing criteria; omit in Direct>
Leverage: <shared mechanism and independent benefits>
Assumptions: <unknowns plus tests>
Decision: <choice, confidence, proposed|accepted|proven|superseded>
Thin slice: <bounded implementation or probe>
Integration: <canonical state/component/production path>
Proof: <signals, tests, renders, or exercised paths>
Links: <prior decision ids or artifacts when relevant>

A Compare or Probe response without the labeled mode, focal question, decision, integration, and proof is incomplete even when its recommendation is sound. Direct work that did not pass the load gate does not need a synthesis block.

Minimum observable content by mode:

  • Compare: mode, question, evidence, options, criteria, leverage, decision, integration, and proof.
  • Probe: all Compare fields plus assumptions, bounded probe, observable signals, expand/stop conditions, and decision status.

Keep the labeled core stable, but allow closely related content to share a field: criteria may sit beside option judgments, the decisive uncertainty may sit in Mode, and integration may be repeated only in the Muriel delta. Do not emit an empty label or duplicate prose merely to satisfy the template.

Do not fabricate fields to make the trace look complete. Mark unknowns honestly. Do not expose private reasoning. The observable object is the decision space, supporting evidence, selected direction, and learning history.

Persist a machine-readable trace only when the calling environment already has an authorized event-log or decision-record sink, or the user requests one. Keep the event shape small and versioned:

{"kind":"muriel.design","version":1,"decisionId":"…","phase":"frame|explore|choose|shape|proof","mode":"direct|compare|probe","status":"proposed|accepted|proven|superseded","summary":"…","evidence":["…"],"links":["…"]}

Do not add a telemetry dependency merely to emit this record. A later logger can reuse the same shape without changing the reasoning contract.

docs.title: Proof and anti-patterns
docs.text:
Judge synthesis by whether it changes a material decision and produces better evidence, not by the number of options, criteria, or trace events.

Before handoff, check:

  • [ ] The mode matches uncertainty and stakes.
  • [ ] Options differ mechanically or structurally, not only cosmetically.
  • [ ] Any provocation names the challenged assumption, option delta, and keep/adapt/drop disposition.
  • [ ] Product truth and authority boundaries remain explicit.
