Access: denied the sheet render, so its denial is real and its Isolation is plain subagent. In ww-1017-m8 it graded "Syrup" HIGH as a claim about the medium that README line 3 contradicts (mineral oil and dyed water), and "Spin" MEDIUM because "spin" reads as playing music on an app with no audio.

Pedants vary on a shared element, and the variation depends on the option set, so it is not noise. ww-1017-k4 graded "Syrup" LOW: it was in all three options and read as a house element. ww-1017-m8 graded it HIGH: beside a figurative rival, it read as a literal claim about the medium. Record both and do not reconcile them. The comparative ranking cannot be moved by an element every option shares, so its severity belongs to the defect union alone.

The Forger — the counterfeit is a name pool. Before opening any option, the seat builds a counterfeit pool from the use statement alone, stamps start and end with date -u +%FT%TZ, and writes it to forgery/<decisionId>/counterfeits.forgery.md. Only then does it open the options. For each, it inventories the name's decisions — construction, casing, length, each lexeme, metaphor source, register, era marker — and diffs each against the pool. F, R, Rs and the severity table are unchanged from the agent definition. The counterfeit sheet is the shared name sheet with a pool name substituted. Pool width, template list and hop distance are fixed by Rule (a) and are not the seat's to choose.

The Thumbnail — the name sheet's downscale companions. Lens: the thumb-eighth companion of the name sheet, with each slot's real size as the intended use size. Judges: truncation in each slot, word shape at the small slots, and how the name skims in a list. Only the 1/8 companion discriminates. At 16 px no word survives on any option, so every option fails there equally and there is no ranking signal in the 16 px reading; record it and recuse from ranking on it.

The Squinter — unseated. Blur keeps position and area and removes the letters. The sheets differ only in the name string, so their blurred renders differ by a few pixels of word length, with no naming signal in them. Record the seat as unseated rather than giving it a costume: a seat without a lens correlates with every other seat.

The Stranger — single-artifact only. The seat is denied the option set, so it cannot rank names. Seat it on one sheet, or on the published page once one exists, for its three questions. Its Ship (this seat's loss only) stays out of the direction ranking, as on any single-artifact ballot.

A naming panel is therefore Pedant, Forger and Thumbnail: three seats, the minimum The chair treats as a real panel. Budget three critiques per option plus one shared counterfeit pool. Expect low concordance. The unhost panel measured 0.33, with the meaning seats and the scale seat anti-correlated, and that split — meaning against legibility — was the finding.

docs.title: Rule (a): a fixed Forger pool
docs.text:
On a name, the Forger's severity moved with the size of its pool. SyrupSpin was rated HIGH against a 30-name pool in ww-1017-k4, where "Syrup" survived as residue, and CRITICAL against a 105-name pool in ww-1017-m8, where "syrup" was scored near, one synonym hop from the pool's "Viscous". Same name, same seat, two severities, and the two pools were also built from different template lists. A severity that moves with the seat's stopping point is a measure of the stopping point. Fix all four inputs:

  • Width — at least 100 names, and at least 6 from every template. That width is reached well inside the four-minute ceiling: the 105-name pool took at most 48 seconds. With a narrower pool, the templates' reach is understated, and that reach is the claim the seat exists to test.
  • Templates — all sixteen, the union of both sittings' lists:
# Template From the sittings 1 Closed compound: substance or texture + effect or motion OilSwirl 2 Open pair: colour or quality adjective + substance noun Neon Oil 3 Portmanteau of two domain words Liquilux 4 Single evocative noun or verb Drift 5 Period, place or venue reference Fillmore 6 Period slang, pun or lyric Far Out 7 Apparatus or medium, literal Overhead 8 Domain technical term Meniscus 9 App suffix or cute-ifier (-ly, -io, -ify, -y, -r) Swirly 10 Latinate or pseudo-classical coinage Lumina 11 Platform or world suffix (-TV, -scape, -verse) GlowTV 12 Echo of the category or subtitle Liquid Dreams 13 Nearest consumer object Lava Light 14 Genre prefix (Psych-, Trip-) Psychlight 15 Rhyme or reduplication Glow Flow 16 Two-word mood phrase Mind Melt
  • Hop distance — one. A lexeme is near when it is a first-page synonym of a pool lexeme, and the diff row names the hop (syrup ← viscous, pool #88). Two hops or more is residue. Without a stated distance, a wider pool and a stricter diff cannot be told apart.
  • Use statement — written once per product. The chair writes it, stores it beside the ledger, and passes it verbatim to every sitting. A later sitting on the same product reuses the earlier pool unchanged and only tops it up to the minimum, so a name that reaches the panel twice is diffed against the same counterfeits both times.

docs.title: Rule (b): no Forger veto
docs.text:
In a naming sitting the option is the string, so a Forger CRITICAL is form-fatal by construction: its only fix is a different name, and a different name is a different option. Applied as written, the form-fatal carve-out amounts to a Forger veto over direction selection — the outcome the carve-out was kept narrow to prevent — resting on the finding shown under Rule (a) to be least stable. In ww-1017-m8 the Forger rated SyrupSpin CRITICAL (R = 0 of F = 16, form_fatal: yes), and under the carve-out that ballot alone would have eliminated it.

In a naming sitting, the chair reports the ranking twice: once over every seated option, and once over the remainder after form-fatal eliminations, naming the finding behind each elimination.

  • If both rankings put the same option first, say so. The elimination changed nothing.
  • If they differ, that is split trigger 6 under Splits are the product: the comparative body prefers an option the defect body fails on form. Route it to the split report with the product question it raises — for a Forger CRITICAL, whether a name a generic template reaches is acceptable for this product — and name no winner.

That option's verdict is still FAIL under the CRITICAL. A name cannot be repaired without becoming another name, so a human who ships it anyway has declined the finding: record the disposition as miss, with the human's stated reason. The rule covers a form-fatal CRITICAL from any seat on a name; the Forger's is the one that is form-fatal every time.

Requiring a second seat to concur before eliminating, on the model of the inline-seat restriction, was the alternative. It fails here. No other seat judges distinctiveness, so concurrence on the same defect could never arrive and the Forger's CRITICAL would be silently capped. Under concurrence on any defect, two unrelated findings could combine into an elimination neither seat claimed. Under the dual report, both bodies' outputs stay intact and the conflict goes to the human, which is what the split report is for.

docs.title: Rule (c): standing context crosses the subagent boundary
docs.text:
The chair's conversation stays on its side of the subagent boundary. What the harness loads into every agent at spawn does not. In Claude Code that includes each CLAUDE.md in scope and the auto-memory index, MEMORY.md, which is loaded into every subagent. The ww-1017-m8 Forger disclosed that the product's working name was in the index before it built its pool, and it flagged the pool items affected. A Stranger spawned into the same context would have been handed project context the protocol denies it.

Before seating:

  1. Search the standing context — every file the harness loads at spawn — for each option string, the working name, and words from the question. A hit is a leak.
  2. Keep pending decisions out of it. While a jury is pending, no candidate name or working name goes into an index line or a CLAUDE.md. A memory about the decision goes in a file the index does not list, or waits until the sitting closes.
  3. Remove the leak or record it. Removing it means moving the line out of the index before seating. If it stays, every seat records Isolation: subagent (denial partial — standing context) and names the leaked string under Evidence seen. The Forger flags pool items that equal or contain the string and counts a template as reaching such an item only when the template produces it without the leak, as the ww-1017-m8 Forger did. A Stranger whose standing context names an option or the question is contaminated: reseat it cleanly or record it unseated, as after an abort.

Instruct every seat to report, before it reads any evidence, whether its own context names an option, the working name, or the question. A seat can see its standing context; the chair cannot see the seat's.

docs.title: Anti-patterns
docs.text:
Do not:

  • Convene a jury on a measurable fact. Contrast, gamut, dimensions, token adherence, and regex-detectable polish rules are settled by tools. A panel deliberating a contrast ratio can get it wrong.
  • Seat N copies of one critic. Same lens, same loss, different adjectives buys correlated errors at one full critique per seat per option. If two seats do not deny each other's evidence or optimize different losses, cut one.
  • Run a jury and muriel-critique on the same artifact. The generalist overlaps four of five seats; the union then counts one defect twice and it reads as corroboration.
  • Claim a denial a scripted prompt cannot enforce. Evidence denial needs a subagent boundary. Inline, mark Isolation: inline (denial nominal) and accept the CRITICAL restriction; never seat the Stranger this way.
  • Stack mutually exclusive fixes in the union. Two seats attacking one target from opposite directions is a split, not two defects, and routing it to the split is the only way the panel can acquit a form that is right.
  • Average away a split. The mean of five rankings discards the finding. The split is the product; the ranking is the byproduct.
  • Let severity inflate. A seat whose every finding is CRITICAL carries zero bits under any-CRITICAL → FAIL. Score dispositions, apply the discount, cap the shouters.
  • Convene on a test render. Panels are for work about to be committed. A draft-DPI intermediate does not earn five seats.
  • Seat a naming panel on whatever names came to mind. The jury cannot add an option. Harvest source material and generate a long list first, and hand the human the long list, not only the shortlist.
  • Let the chair vote. A chair with a preference is a sixth juror holding procedural power, and it will resolve splits it was meant to report.
  • Show round 1 ballots to a juror still voting. That measures conformity.
  • Skip Order seen. Without the recorded permutation you cannot separate judgement from position bias, and the panel does not replay.
  • Let a seat recuse from nothing, or run a Delphi round to manufacture agreement. A seat that judges everything correlates with every other generalist; movement nobody can source to specific evidence is deference.

docs.title: Prior art
docs.text: Adapt from the design-school crit and the award jury, which get the structure right and the measurement wrong. Right: a chair who owns the question rather than an opinion; a stated brief the work is judged against; recusal when a juror has a stake; reasoning voiced before the score is committed. Wrong: halo and star effects contaminate every subsequent criterion once one juror names a favorite; the loudest or most senior voice dominates because deliberation is public from the first minute; and absolute rubric scores show poor inter-rater reliability across juries and across sittings. Comparative judgement — Thurstone's law of comparative judgement via Bradley-Terry, as deployed in educational assessment — exists largely because absolute-scoring juries in education proved unreliable, and it yields the reliability statistic as a side effect of the binary decisions. The sealed first round is the fix for public deliberation; the Delphi round with a who-moved record is the fix for treating convergence as evidence.

docs.title: Milliseconds matter — design the routines people can adopt
docs.text: Use for repeated interactions, information access, direct manipulation, or a novel control whose value depends on how perception, thought, and action fit together. Carry the relevant insight into the existing synthesis and working artifact. Load this reference selectively alongside the primary channel.

docs.title: What the research contributes
docs.text:
Gray and Boehm-Davis (2000) analyze microstrategies: small arrangements of cognitive, perceptual, and motor operations. Their CPM-GOMS models represent dependencies and overlap; the critical path determines predicted duration. In their button experiment, a predictable return location supported earlier movement than an unknown next target. Their separate two-person prototype study used model discrepancies to diagnose possible cue and verification problems. Those diagnoses were hypotheses, rather than experimentally confirmed causes. Their framing joins embodied cognition, task, and artifact.

Gray and Fu (2004) distinguish what an interface permits from the costs that favor one routine over another. In two experiments, access costs encouraged use of imperfect memory despite accurate external information, with worse performance. External availability alone did not determine information use.

Gray, Sims, Fu, and Schoelles (2006) tested temporal resource tradeoffs through three Blocks World experiments and an Ideal Performer Model. Their account opposes a universal preference to conserve memory. It concerns local interactive routines; locally economical behavior need not produce the best overall result.

docs.title: Put the insight into the interaction
docs.text:
These are design applications to test in the host product:

  • Map a consequential routine: finding information, acquiring a target, recalling context, acting, waiting, checking, and continuing. Ask which steps depend on others and which could overlap. A click count misses these choices.
  • Compare the cost of consulting external information with remembering or guessing. Consider reveal gestures, gaze travel, window changes, waiting, and returning to the task. Make information practical to use where it matters.
  • Inspect predictability and state cues. Can people prepare the next action? Is a pause useful verification, uncertainty, or an interface-imposed wait?
  • Explore inventions that change these relationships: an adjacent comparison, persistent reference, stable target, or preview during direct manipulation. Name the routine the candidate enables and the tradeoff it introduces.
  • Observe the strategy as well as elapsed time: consulting, recalling, rechecking, errors, and recovery. Compare early use with practiced use when skill acquisition matters. Treat inferred internal operations as hypotheses.

For example, compare a delayed hover reveal with an adjacent persistent value in a tuning tool. Predict whether people will consult the value or estimate from memory; observe consultation, accuracy, and interference with the task. This proposed comparison is an extrapolation, not a result of Gray's studies.

docs.title: Interpretation limits
docs.text: These studies inform routine interaction, not a universal objective to minimize time. Preserve useful verification and meaningful task goals. Do not copy their operator durations into modern performance budgets or invent a savings estimate. Model estimates need stated assumptions; measured benefits need task evidence. The interaction-contract response budgets answer a different question: how the product acknowledges and reports work.

docs.title: Sources and intake basis
docs.text:
• Gray, W. D., and Boehm-Davis, D. A. (2000). Milliseconds matter: An introduction to microstrategies and to their use in describing and predicting interactive behavior. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Applied, 6(4), 322–335. Intake: author-posted manuscript, including methods, models, and discussion.
  • Gray, W. D., and Fu, W.-T. (2004). Soft constraints in interactive behavior: the case of ignoring perfect knowledge in-the-world for imperfect knowledge in-the-head. Cognitive Science, 28(3), 359–382. Intake: publisher abstract; the summary above stays at that scope.
  • Gray, W. D., Sims, C. R., Fu, W.-T., and Schoelles, M. J. (2006). The soft constraints hypothesis: A rational analysis approach to resource allocation for interactive behavior. Psychological Review, 113(3), 461–482. Intake: author-posted full-text sections on the hypothesis, experimental-data limits, and conclusions. All three records verified against Crossref.

docs.title: Motion craft — staging, expression, and continuity
docs.text: Use when motion needs an authored character, several elements must communicate one change, or prepared imagery follows live input. Load from the polish, interactive, or video channel; a routine transition needs only its existing recipe. This reference informs design within the host's current animation stack.

docs.title: Keep the clock and the contract
docs.text:
Polish rules, muriel.motion, and the host's compliant brand tokens remain authoritative: utility transitions stay at or below 100 ms, cinematic transitions at or above 1500 ms. Keep the existing hold, spring, and press distinctions, sequence budgets, easing directions, scale limits, and reduced-motion policies. This reference adds no timing bands or exemptions. Do not stretch routine feedback into the cinematic bucket to accommodate a borrowed recipe.

Use interaction contracts for state ownership, acknowledgment, cancellation, and recovery. Animation completion must not imply an operation succeeded. Expressive motion must preserve access to controls and the host's actual state.

docs.title: Give motion a specific job
docs.text:
Name what the viewer should notice: an object's destination, a relationship, a changed status, a material transformation, or a deliberate expressive moment. Then choose a property and path that carry that meaning. A moving object can retain its identity across a layout change; a reveal can expose a relationship; a settled pose can make a result available for inspection.

For expressive work, translate a few words from the brief into concrete choices within the existing rules: restrained displacement, a consistent origin, controlled arcs, coordinated arrival, or a distinctive resting pose. Reuse those choices for related actions. Brand character can live in geometry, amplitude, and composition while the timing tokens stay fixed. Follow the host's easing semantics; do not replace them with a universal signature curve.

Treat associations such as curved movement suggesting warmth as design hypotheses to inspect in context. Do not assign a stock personality to an entire product category or claim a motion recipe reliably produces an emotion.

docs.title: Choreograph relationships
docs.text:
• Stage the meaningful change around one focal action. Supporting movement is optional and should make that action easier to follow; a quiet background is a valid composition. Keep Muriel's one load-bearing motion per interaction.
  • Derive origins and destinations from relationships: a panel from its trigger, an item toward its new location, a detail from its parent. Preserve stable anchors where the viewer needs to compare before and after.
  • Sequence by dependency or reading order when that relationship matters. Elements expressing one event may arrive together. Do not stagger every list or impose a screen-fraction rule on how many elements may move.
  • Use anticipation or follow-through only where it earns its place. A narrative reveal may benefit from preparation and settlement; a repeated command needs immediate acknowledgment. Optional secondary cues must obey the same timing, scale, and spring rules and must not delay access to the result.
  • Let the result settle into a readable state. Keep important labels and values available for comparison; preserve text contrast instead of dimming unrelated content to manufacture emphasis. Judge a repeated interaction after repeated use, when surprise has worn off.

docs.title: Separate input, playback, and material
docs.text:
For interactive media, resolve these choices independently in the existing interaction contract. Page layout or a file extension does not decide them.

Choice Design question Input Which pointer, scroll, touch, keyboard, data, or application-state change drives it? Playback Does input continuously select a frame, select a transition that plays, or start/stop autonomous playback? State space Is the material a bounded progression, a cycle, independent states, or genuinely two-dimensional variation? Composition Does the scene belong inside the media, or must the subject combine with the host page?

Continuous control should retain its correspondence with input. A transition selected by input needs an explicit interruption policy: retarget, queue, or ignore for a stated task reason. When reversal is supported, continue from the currently visible position rather than restarting a clip. Do not add cosmetic lag to direct manipulation; any scheduled settling follows the existing motion policy. A horizontal sweep cannot also represent independent vertical variation.

Keep product state in its canonical owner. A media manifest may describe frames, segment boundaries, and mappings to existing state IDs; it must not become a second application state machine. Derive media times from the processed output and update them when trimming or re-encoding changes the sequence.

docs.title: Make the material hold together
docs.text:
Use native transforms or procedural rendering for changes they can express faithfully. Prepared media is useful when pose, occlusion, material, or structure changes require authored frames. Generated imagery used to explain a real mechanism needs reference checks for that mechanism as well as visual continuity.

For a media sequence:

  • Record what must stay consistent about subject identity, proportions, anchor, lighting, and background ownership. Inspect adjoining frames after processing; continuity depends on the displayed result, not just compatible prompts or planned poses.
  • For a generated chain, use the accepted output endpoint as the next segment's starting reference when the production tool supports it. Check the resulting join again; matching input images alone cannot establish a seamless output.
  • Choose delivery using real display dimensions, pixel density, decoded memory, and access pattern. An atlas can suit frequent random access; video can suit a longer progression. Measure seek and reversal behavior on the target device.
  • Complete one representative segment in the actual host before producing a larger set. Include its transition to rest and, for interactive work, input reversal and the static alternative. Fix wrong subject structure or movement in the source material.

Keep existing generation providers, renderers, and media tools. These ideas do not require installing either upstream skill or adopting its service defaults.

docs.title: Inspect the experience
docs.text:
Select checks that match the work:

  • At normal speed, can the intended change and its destination be followed? Inspect sequence boundaries as well as isolated attractive frames.
  • Exercise rapid reversal, interruption, repeated input, and keyboard/touch equivalents. Check that old playback cannot overwrite a newer state.
  • Repeat common actions: does choreography become waiting, distraction, or an obstacle to comparison? Simplify the sequence within the existing timing rules.
  • Check narrow layouts, actual display size, initial loading, media failure, and reduced motion. Disable continuous input-driven animation when the chosen fallback is static; turning off easing alone still allows frame changes.
  • Preserve the complete current state in the accessible alternative. Explanatory figures retain Muriel's complete final frame for reduced motion, no-JS, print, and static export. Keep essential information outside motion-only cues.

Rendered and interaction checks establish artifact behavior. Claims about comprehension, workload, or emotional response need appropriate human evidence.

docs.title: Sources and adaptation
docs.text:
Craft inspiration, reviewed 2026-10-16; these are design precedents rather than empirical authority for numerical limits. The guidance above is written for Muriel; no upstream code, media, or dependencies are included.

  • LottieFiles motion-design-skill: motion identity, choreography, and quality review inform expressive consistency, staging, and repeated-use inspection. Its core prescriptions for duration bands, mandatory motion layers, overshoot, opacity combinations, and screen-fraction limits are not adopted.
  • oil-motion: runtime semantics, delivery selection, and production workflow inform independent input/playback choices, continuity checks, resource-aware delivery, and a representative pilot. Muriel keeps the host's canonical state, production tooling, accessibility contract, and timing rules.

docs.title: Multiscale adapters — join the host's state
docs.text: Read after multiscale coordination when choosing or integrating a renderer. These are integration recipes, not another framework. Use the project's installed library version and canonical query/state paths. The Linked Atlas implements the invariant core in native ES modules; the library-specific snippets below are sketches to adapt and test in the host, not validated drop-in adapters.

docs.title: Choose the smallest useful substrate
docs.text:
Host Good fit Work still owned by the product DOM / SVG with D3 Custom spatial grammar, moderate mark counts, explicit gestures Canonical selection, representation levels, aggregate membership, accessible controls Vega-Lite Declarative linked analytical views, reproducible chart specifications Cross-dataset identity, application state bridge, accessible workflows, semantic-level orchestration ECharts Existing dashboards with dataZoom/brush and many chart types Stable ID mapping, filter/viewport distinction, feedback-loop protection Canvas / WebGL Dense scenes, large fields, expensive geometry Hit testing, spatial indexes, semantic DOM companion, data-space predicates Existing native UI A native product with established navigation and accessibility Translate the same contract into its state and input system; no web rewrite required

Do not choose by an invented universal row-count cutoff. Measure the actual mark geometry, labels, visible subset, query cost, hardware, and update cadence.

docs.title: D3: gestures are adapters, scales are derived
docs.text:
D3 brush extents and selections use SVG coordinates. Invert the current scales before dispatching a domain query. brush.move can generate brush events; sourceEvent identifies the underlying input event. Choose an explicit guard for renderer-driven synchronization. D3 brush.

Sketch for a one-dimensional selection brush, with the host supplying dispatch, xDetail, and the current selection operation:

let reflecting = false;
const brush = d3.brushX().on('end.model', (event) => {
  if (reflecting) return;
  if (event.selection === null) {
    dispatch({type: 'selection.clear'});
    return;
  }
  const bounds = event.selection.map(xDetail.invert).map(Number).sort((a,b) => a-b);
  dispatch({type: 'selection.query', field: 'time', bounds,
    operation: selectedOperation(), source: 'detail'});
});

function reflectBrush(pixelBounds) {
  reflecting = true;
  try { brushGroup.call(brush.move, pixelBounds); }
  finally { reflecting = false; }
}

This immediate synchronization guard does not cover a transition scheduled to emit events later. Prefer immediate reflection during input. If transitions are necessary, retain an origin/revision token for their full lifetime. For live brushing, dispatch a pending predicate during movement and one commit at the end; preserve the starting selection for set composition and cancellation.

Keep an untransformed base scale. D3's rescaleX / rescaleY derive display scales from a zoom transform. zoom.transform emits events and does not enforce scale/translation extents; validate restored transforms or use the constrained convenience operations. D3 zoom.

If the brush group is inside a transformed group, establish its local coordinate frame explicitly. Never invert once through the scale and again through the same zoom. Resize updates scale ranges, gesture extents, and projected brush geometry together; retain the data-domain query. Assert the same selected IDs after a CSS resize, nonzero SVG viewBox origin, and browser device-scale change.

docs.title: Vega-Lite: specify selection and scale resolution independently
docs.text:
Current selection parameters support point and interval, with global, union, or intersect resolution across repeated views. Projection over aggregated fields is limited to its defining view. Interval projections over binned/time-unit fields remain continuous. Selection parameters.

Make the intended role explicit in the spec. For example, a scatter view can highlight members of a region while retaining the rest as context:

{
  "params": [{"name": "region", "select": {
    "type": "interval", "encodings": ["x", "y"], "resolve": "global"
  }}],
  "mark": "point",
  "encoding": {
    "x": {"field": "time", "type": "quantitative"},
    "y": {"field": "value", "type": "quantitative"},
    "size": {"condition": {"param": "region", "empty": false, "value": 100},
             "value": 30}
  }
}

Here empty: false belongs to the consuming predicate. Explicitly add the host's accessible status and controls; size is only a supplementary selection cue. A filtering consumer instead uses a filter transform, which changes its population and denominator. Check whether that consumer should show all records or zero records when the brush is inactive. Parameter predicates.

An interval bound to scales controls navigation. It is not automatically a selected cohort. Use separate parameters for navigation and selection; resolve scale sharing independently of selection sharing. Scale binding, scale resolution.

If the surrounding application owns selection, use a documented public View API bridge and a defined origin guard. Avoid a React state copy plus a Vega signal copy that can disagree. Do not rely on undocumented compiler-generated signal names as a cross-version protocol. For a one-way specification, the Vega view can itself be the single owner; choose ownership deliberately. Vega View API.

docs.title: ECharts: translate indices at the data boundary
docs.text:
ECharts exposes input events and actions through on and dispatchAction. Actions can update linked chart state; explicit event handling is also available. Event and action guide.

Keep a stable id alongside each source record and a revisioned mapping from each rendered series index to that ID. Resolve reported indices against the exact dataset that produced the event. Sorting, filtering, transforms, and aggregation can change index meaning. For aggregate marks, resolve to member IDs or a documented predicate rather than selecting the bin's display index.

Treat dataZoom and brush as separate product actions. Review dataZoom's filtering mode before interpreting a view as a fixed-population viewport. Route selection feedback through guarded actions or derived styling; do not bounce events between charts indefinitely. Avoid recreating options on each pointer move when an overlay or a bounded style update suffices.

Read the installed version's brush options, dataZoom options, and API before wiring payloads. These pages are dynamically rendered; the event guide alone does not verify every version's brush payload shape. Test your chosen series types with a known-ID fixture.

docs.title: Canvas / WebGL: selection belongs to data
docs.text:
Convert client coordinates into the plot's CSS coordinate system, then through the inverse camera/scale. Device-pixel ratio belongs to raster resolution; do not apply it a second time to DOM pointer positions. For rotated/perspective scenes, use the actual inverse transform or ray intersection rather than a bounding-box approximation. Keep clipping, axis inversion, and logarithmic domains in the same transform used for drawing.

Build the spatial index from stable data, or invalidate a screen-space index whenever its transform changes. A bounding rectangle can produce candidates for a lasso, but final membership needs the polygon predicate. GPU picking IDs map back to entity IDs; they are not persistent identities themselves.

Use separate budgets for visible marks, semantic labels, accessible DOM elements, and data queries. Rendering fewer marks must not silently reduce the selection universe. If interaction uses sampled data or approximate queries, label that scope, keep exact and approximate results distinct, and reconcile without presenting an estimate as a completed exact selection.

Retain keyboard focus independently of pooled visual nodes. A focused or pinned entity needs a stable DOM inspection route even when its mark is offscreen or represented by an aggregate. Provide a list/table and the same named actions through ordinary controls; do not make thousands of marks individual tab stops.

docs.title: Adapter acceptance
docs.text:
For the chosen host, verify a small fixture before optimizing:

  1. A gesture and its form/keyboard equivalent return the same IDs.
  2. The same IDs survive sorting, resizing, zooming, and representation changes.
  3. Programmatic reflection emits no new user commit or infinite event loop.
  4. Clear and an active zero-match query remain distinguishable.
  5. A stale query response cannot replace a newer accepted result.
  6. Filtering and panning have the stated effect on counts and hidden selection.
  7. Destroy/remount removes old listeners and preserves only intended state.

Use the evaluation fixtures for independent expected answers. A library's built-in brush or animation proves neither these invariants nor a benefit to the analyst.

docs.title: Semantic zoom, linked displays, and brushing
docs.text:
Use this reference when the task needs people to move between scales, select a subset in one representation, and inspect its meaning in another. Read the interactive channel first. Use multiscale adapters for the host's rendering library and zooming interfaces for continuous canvases, spatial collections, camera behavior, and navigation recovery.

Muriel's job is to design the representations and their coordination. Begin with a real question: “Which observations make this cluster unusual, and does that relationship persist over time?” A page of independently interactive charts does not answer it until the relationships between their states are defined, visible, and exercised.

The research lineage is documented in the repository's research/semantic-zoom-linked-views.md and research/multiscale-history.md, with a verified bibliography. The contracts below are engineering and design recommendations derived from that lineage. Their exact thresholds, gestures, and layouts require calibration in the host; they are not experimentally established constants. Open the linked atlas for the runnable teaching implementation and its model and interaction tests; use multiscale evaluation to exercise the capability.

The core lineage is Pad++ and space-scale diagrams for representation at scale; brushing scatterplots for coordinated selection; Snap-Together for relational coordination; and Vega-Lite for explicit selection semantics. These are design, formalism, and system foundations. The overview/detail review and transition experiments help bound claims: performance depends on tasks and conditions; neither motion nor an additional view guarantees better analysis.

docs.title: 1. Choose the mechanism by the work
docs.text:
Mechanism What changes Use when Question to resolve Geometric zoom Magnification and visible extent Spatial detail needs inspection What remains a stable landmark? Semantic zoom Representation changes with usable scale An overview and an item need different encodings What becomes meaningful at each level? Details on demand Information about an indicated entity appears Exact values or provenance are occasional needs Does inspection require disturbing the viewport? Drilldown Dataset scope or hierarchy level changes The task follows a parent/child relation How are scope and the return path shown? Overview + detail Context and focus occupy separate regions Location and detail must be compared What navigation is linked, and in which direction? Focus + context Detail is embedded in surrounding context A local lens helps a spatial task Does distortion undermine metric comparisons or targeting? Linked brushing A selected subset is represented across views Complementary attributes need comparison What identity or relationship links the records? Crossfiltering A query changes other views' input populations The task narrows a cohort Does the originating view retain its full context?

These can be combined, but each adds behavior the person must learn. A cluster expanding into its members is semantic zoom if representation depends on scale. Clicking it to replace the dataset is drilldown. A tooltip is details on demand. Enlarging unchanged labels is geometric zoom. Describe the mechanism accurately before claiming a semantic-zoom capability.

Give every view one analytic job and a reason to exist. A useful combination is a distribution overview, an alternative projection, an exact record table, and a pinned inspector. A second scatterplot with different axes can be valuable; three copies of the same summary usually cannot justify their space.

docs.title: 2. Write the coordination contract before rendering
docs.text:
Record these decisions in the host's design note or implementation:

Concern Required declaration Identity Entity namespace, stable key, dataset version, duplicate-key policy Selection universe Whole dataset, eligible filtered records, or visible records Selection meaning Frozen IDs or a live predicate; empty and absent behavior Relationship Same entities, parent/child, membership, join, or another declared mapping Viewport Per-view domains/transform; explicit synchronization groups Aggregation Grouping fields, membership, denominator, overlap, missingness Brush Fields, units, bounds, operation, commit/cancel behavior Preview and pin Ephemeral inspection versus persistent reference Filter Which views and denominators it changes; how it is removed Resolution How simultaneous brushes combine across views Recovery Clear selection, clear filter, reset viewport, undo, restore

One canonical state does not require a new global-store library. Join the host's existing reducer, signals, query model, or controller. Keep renderer-local state limited to drawing, hit testing, and an in-progress gesture. A possible shape:

{
  dataVersion: 'observations-v3',
  revision: 17,
  filters: { category: null },
  selection: null, // or { kind: 'ids', ids: [] } or a typed predicate
  preview: null,   // { namespace: 'observation', id: 'o-31' }
  pin: null,
  viewports: { spatial: { x: [0, 100], y: [0, 100] } },
  brushes: {},     // authored predicates + provenance; not authoritative pixels
  interaction: { tool: 'brush', operation: 'replace' }
}

Selection, filter, pin, hover, and viewport are different state dimensions. Panning does not change the selected entities unless the product explicitly offers “select visible.” Hovering does not silently replace a pin. Clearing a brush does not reset the viewport. Show these differences in the controls and state readout, not only in variable names.

Expose named commands and read-only diagnostics for automated exercise. The diagnostic snapshot should contain IDs, extents, level, counts, and revisions; tests should also use the actual input routes. A debug API alone cannot prove the visible controls work.

docs.title: 3. Design a representation ladder
docs.text:
For each level, specify the task, available evidence, mark semantics, allowed actions, and transition criterion. Prefer a few consequential changes over many cosmetic levels. A specimen ladder for an observation atlas:

Level Representation Human question Selection meaning Overview Stable spatial bins with counts and spread Where are concentrations and exceptions? Select members of a bin, or explicitly brush raw positions Neighborhood Individual marks plus restrained group context Which observations form the apparent pattern? Select stable observation IDs Detail Records with measured labels and available attributes Which entity is this, and what supports its value? Same IDs; inspect or pin without replacing the cohort

The ladder need not end in cards, and every view need not change level at once. A timeline may aggregate by time while a map groups by location. Declare each view's semantic level and maintain the correspondence through identity.

Measure the available screen space. Use projected mark spacing, measured label dimensions, plot area, overlap, and visible mark count. Raw zoom k is a poor portable threshold: the same k produces different affordances after a resize. For one-dimensional spacing, pixelsPerUnit = plotWidth / domainSpan. For nonuniform or nonlinear layouts, measure projected bounds locally. Text must meet Muriel's size and contrast rules; shrink the information budget before shrinking prose below them.

Use hysteresis. Enter detail only when the footprint clears an upper threshold; leave it below a lower threshold. Retain the current level in the gap. For example, entering at 60 px and leaving at 45 px is an illustrative policy to calibrate, not a perception result. Apply the rule to each adjacent level and test oscillation, large jumps, and resize. If a collision budget is exceeded, prioritize labels deterministically; do not continually reshuffle them on every pointer movement.

Preserve evidence across the boundary. A coarse bin must retain its member IDs or an exact membership predicate. An individual outlier must not vanish from the analytic result because its label is hidden. Show the binning or aggregation rule, count, units, missing values, and relevant uncertainty. A mean alone can conceal a bimodal population; choose the overview statistic for the task and provide inspection of its members.

docs.title: 4. Preserve navigation anchors and identity
docs.text:
For an affine world-to-screen transform screen = k * world + t, preserve the world point below the zoom anchor a:

worldAtAnchor = (a - t) / k
tNext         = a - kNext * worldAtAnchor

Apply independently to x and y after accounting for plot offsets. For scale domains, use the inverse scale at the anchor and solve the new domain around that value. Log scales require the scale's transform/inverse; geographic projections and rotated cameras need their actual geometry. Bounds clamping may prevent exact anchoring at an edge: make that constraint deliberate and test the unconstrained invariant separately from the boundary policy.

At a semantic transition, maintain stable spatial landmarks, parent/member relationships, selection, and pin identity. A transition may show a group expanding toward members when the grouping supports that correspondence. Do not morph unrelated entities into one another merely because their screen positions are nearby. Make an immediate reduced-motion route equally legible.

When detail controls or labels appear, preserve keyboard focus by entity ID. If a focused entity is no longer drawable, keep its inspector or transfer focus to a named surviving control; do not drop it onto the document body. Back or reset should restore a meaningful context. A persistent overview, named path, or saved view can be more useful than an elaborate camera animation.

docs.title: 5. Treat brushing as a query with an explicit lifetime
docs.text:
Convert pointer coordinates through the current plot transform into data-space bounds. Normalize drag direction, then evaluate membership against the declared universe. Use one specified boundary rule; for contiguous bins, half-open intervals avoid double inclusion, with an explicit final-domain endpoint rule. Handle reversed scales, missing values, dates/time zones, log domains, and degenerate extents. A zero-size drag may be a point pick or an empty brush; make that gesture distinction explicit.

Store persistent extents in data coordinates. Reproject them on zoom and resize. The screen rectangle is a view of the predicate, not the predicate itself. For lassos and irregular projections, retain the proper geometry and coordinate reference; an inverted bounding rectangle may not describe the drawn region.

For existing set S and current brush match set B:

Operation Result Replace B Add S ∪ B Subtract S \ B Intersect S ∩ B

Take a snapshot S₀ at gesture start. Each preview computes operation(S₀, Bₜ). Do not repeatedly compose against the previous preview: shrinking an additive brush must remove points that were only inside an earlier preview. Commit once on completion; Escape, pointer cancellation, or lost capture restores the snapshot. Freeze the operation during the gesture unless mid-drag modifier changes are an intentionally designed and tested feature.

Absent is not empty. selection: null means no active selection; { kind: 'ids', ids: [] } means an active selection matching nothing. Filtering by the former leaves the eligible population; filtering by the latter returns zero. Never use ids.length === 0 as “show everything.” Disable Add/Subtract/ Intersect until a baseline exists, or document a precise initial-set policy. “No brush” is not automatically the universal set for all operations.

Choose snapshot or live semantics. Frozen IDs keep a cohort stable if data values change. A stored predicate reruns on new data and may select different members. Neither is universally correct. Label the behavior, retain query provenance, and define migration on dataset replacement. When compound selection no longer equals the latest rectangle, show the operation history or cohort summary; do not present that rectangle as the full selected set.

docs.title: 6. Coordinate views through meaning
docs.text:
Views of the same entities exchange stable keys, never array offsets, SVG indices, screen coordinates, or display labels. Sorts, filters, and virtualization must not change identity. Namespace IDs when distinct datasets can contain the same key. Reject duplicate IDs or explicitly model occurrence identity before enabling linking.

Views of related datasets need a declared relation. For customers and orders, brushing customers might select their orders by a customer key; the reverse mapping might select customers with any brushed order. These mappings are not inverses, and counts describe different entity types. For many-to-many relations, define deduplication and aggregation before counting. For probabilistic matches, show uncertainty rather than asserting exact identity. If no defensible relation exists, keep the views unlinked.

A brush in one projection is not a screen rectangle to copy into another. Evaluate its predicate where it was authored, then project matching IDs in the other view. If both views share a domain dimension, a meaningful range overlay can also be drawn in each view's own scale. Shared time axes are useful for temporal comparison; a map, scatterplot, and table can coordinate without a shared coordinate system.

For aggregate mark g with eligible member set Mᵍ and selected set S, derive selectedCount = |Mᵍ ∩ S|. Render none, partial, and full states distinctly, and show the actual counts. Define whether “full” means all eligible or all original members. A 3 of 12 label is more truthful than painting the entire bin as selected. Overlapping groups cannot be summed as though they were a partition. Aggregates based on samples must not imply complete membership.

Choose view query policy intentionally:

Policy Population shown Useful effect Highlight Eligible records remain; selection changes emphasis Preserves comparison with nonmembers Filter Only matching records feed the view Makes the cohort inspectable Context + subset Both full and selected aggregate layers Shows changed composition and denominator Crossfilter except self All relevant predicates except this view's own Retains context for adjusting its filter

Keep hover preview, keyboard focus, pinned inspection, and selected cohort visually distinguishable. Use stable semantic color assignments plus outlines, patterns, shape, labels, or selected-count marks. A pin outside the current filter should say so; it should not disappear silently. A selected cohort outside the viewport still exists and needs a visible count or return action.

docs.title: 7. Make input ownership, access, and recovery explicit
docs.text:
Dragging cannot simultaneously mean pan and brush. Provide a visible tool switch or another unambiguous grammar, plus buttons for operations that would otherwise depend on modifiers. Use pointer capture for drags; handle cancellation and release outside the plot. Decide how a second touch changes or cancels a gesture. Preserve ordinary page scrolling and browser zoom outside the intended interaction surface.

Provide usable alternatives, not a sentence saying “keyboard supported”:

  • Numeric/date bounds and category controls create the same predicates as a brush.
  • Zoom buttons, a reset control, and navigable records support inspection without a wheel.
  • A selectable table or structured list exposes the same eligible/selected IDs.
  • Preview content is available by focus or explicit inspection, not hover alone.
  • A visible operation control supports touch and single-pointer use without modifiers.
  • Escape cancels a gesture; clear selection and reset viewport remain separate.

Keyboard equivalence and a single-pointer alternative to dragging are distinct requirements. W3C's dragging guidance and color guidance inform this implementation. Muriel's 8:1 text-contrast policy remains in force. Small data marks need an accessible inspection path; expanding thousands of overlapping hit targets does not create an intelligible interface.

Announce committed selection counts and level changes using a restrained status region. Avoid narrating every pointer move. Use a manageable focus model rather than thousands of tab stops. Test keyboard and touch completion of the actual analytic question, browser magnification, reduced motion, and a narrow layout. On narrow screens, a persistent cohort summary and explicit view switch can preserve coordination when simultaneous display is impractical.

docs.title: 8. Keep rendering responsive without weakening semantics
docs.text:
Compute from a canonical snapshot, render the affected views, then expose a consistent revision. Prevent programmatic view updates from re-emitting user actions into a coordination loop. Use origin tags or adapter suppression with cleanup, and guard no-op updates. A transaction should publish once even if several dependent views update.

Coalesce input rendering to animation frames. Separate cheap brush/hover feedback from expensive data queries. Culling, level of detail, and label suppression reduce drawing cost; they must not silently reduce the population being queried. Use a spatial index or worker when measured data size requires one. A sampled visual overview needs explicit sampling semantics.

For asynchronous computation, send a request ID plus dataset and query/viewport revision. Accept results only when the versions they depend on still match. Abort superseded work when possible, but use version checking even with aborts. Track dependencies precisely so an unrelated hover does not invalidate a long query. A stale result may remain visibly marked while new work runs; never present mixed revisions as a coherent current analysis.

Measure input-to-feedback, query completion, and settled render separately on representative devices and datasets. Report distributions and the tested size. “60 fps” does not establish correct brushing, exact counts, or usable analysis.

docs.title: 9. Verify invariants, then evaluate the human task
docs.text:
Use deterministic fixtures that include duplicate coordinates, zero matches, missing values, boundary values, outliers, and partial aggregates. Derive expected IDs independently of the renderer. Required checks for implemented capabilities include:

Invariant or behavior Exercise Anchored navigation Compare the world point under an off-center anchor before/after zoom; test edge clamping separately Representation continuity Cross every level in both directions; pin and selection retain identity Hysteresis Oscillate around thresholds and resize through them without level chatter Coordinate correctness Brush after zoom, pan, resize, reversed-axis and transformed-scale changes Selection algebra Replace, union, subtract, intersect; shrink a gesture preview; cancel and undo Empty semantics Active zero matches filters to zero; clearing the brush restores absence Aggregate truth Partial/full/none membership and denominators remain correct at every level Query scope Offscreen selected IDs and filter-hidden pins remain accounted for Coordination All views agree on eligible and selected IDs for the same revision Relationship mapping One-to-many and many-to-many joins count the declared entity type without duplication Event ownership One drag creates one action; programmatic redraw cannot recurse Async freshness Delayed older results cannot overwrite a newer query or dataset Recovery Pointer cancellation, Escape, clear, reset, and restoration have their specified effects Access Equivalent bounds/selection via keyboard and non-drag pointer controls; visible focus and noncolor state

The example's tests demonstrate its supported subset of this contract. They do not establish capability for an unimplemented lasso, projection, streaming dataset, or join. A rendered screenshot proves visible state at a moment; an interaction test proves the exercised path; neither proves understanding.

For human evaluation, compare plausible alternatives on representative tasks: find a cross-view outlier, explain a cluster's members, form and refine a cohort, recover from a mistaken operation, and return to an earlier finding. Compare task success, explanation errors, cohort errors, completion time, recovery, and learning across repeated use. Observe whether people notice level changes and understand partial aggregates. Test with the users and access needs the product serves. Treat reduced workload, improved comprehension, and faster analysis as hypotheses until those outcomes have relevant human evidence.

docs.title: Evaluating semantic zoom, linked displays, and brushing
docs.text:
Use this battery when changing Muriel's multiscale guidance or building an interface whose task depends on coordinated views. It tests whether the skill produces useful working behavior across domains. A passing reference demo is evidence for that demo; it does not establish that a future build, a different dataset, or Muriel's general capability passes.

Read the coordination contract for the design mechanisms, zooming interfaces for navigable spaces and return paths, and the adapters for host integration. The linked-atlas lab supplies one inspectable implementation. The independent fixtures below deliberately cover additional data shapes that the lab does not represent.

docs.title: Four kinds of evidence
docs.text:
Keep these separate in the handoff. A failure in one cannot be repaired by accumulating passes in another.

Evidence What to exercise What a pass establishes Model Small independent data oracles, predicates, ID joins, transforms, event ordering The declared state and aggregation semantics hold for the tested cases Browser interaction Actual pointer, keyboard, focus, wheel, and touch routes; rendered state read back from the page The UI invokes those semantics through the tested input paths Rendered inspection Relevant sizes and tiers, selection/filter combinations, empty/loading/error states, text/mark contrast The inspected outputs are legible and communicate the intended state Human task observation Representative tasks with unfamiliar users; a comparison when claiming improvement What those participants understood or accomplished under the observed conditions

Calling a reducer from a browser console is model evidence. Synthetic pointer events can exercise handlers but do not establish hit testing, pointer capture, native scrolling, or physical touch acceptance. A screenshot does not establish keyboard access. Automated accessibility checks do not establish screen-reader comprehension. Record skipped and unavailable checks explicitly.

The repository includes focused checks for the linked-atlas implementation:

node --test tests/multiscale-coordination.test.mjs
node tests/multiscale-browser.mjs

The browser suite needs Playwright and its Chromium runtime in the test environment. PLAYWRIGHT_MODULE can point to an existing installation, while BASE_URL can supply an already-served lab. Otherwise the script starts and stops its own loopback server. Set SCREENSHOT_DIR to retain captures for a separate rendered inspection. Browser touch checks use Chromium input emulation; physical-device and assistive-technology acceptance remain separate. These checks exercise the reference lab, not all the independent briefs below. The browser suite also checks its rendered HTML and SVG text against the painted background at glyph locations, including SVG label backplates and halos, with an 8:1 floor. Planted low-contrast fills and changed backgrounds verify that the audit can fail. This audit is scoped to the lab's solid-color text; it does not establish chart-mark contrast, native popup-menu contrast, or general image-text accessibility.

docs.title: Run the capability battery
docs.text:
Run the build briefs below in fresh sessions against a recorded skill revision. Give the agent the brief and fixture, with the required task and existing host constraints. Keep the expected answers available to the evaluator. Require a runnable artifact, its canonical-state description, and bounded evidence for what was verified. Preserve the resulting artifacts and event traces, including failed builds.

Evaluate the output, not the presence of vocabulary in its rationale. A response that says "semantic zoom" while enlarging the same marks fails the relevant task. A modest table with the required correspondence and recovery can pass a linking task without using a prescribed library or visual form.

For each brief report pass, fail, or not observed against its listed behaviors. Record the first reproducible counterexample and user consequence. Do not turn mixed evidence into an invented quality score. Repeat fresh runs when estimating reliability; report runs completed / runs attempted and the number passing each behavior. Fix the fixture before comparing skill revisions when a task or oracle proves ambiguous.

docs.title: A. Time-series cohort investigation
docs.text:
Brief: Build a small investigation surface for field observations. Let a reader select a time window, compare its habitat composition, inspect individual records, and retain a chosen record while changing the viewport and habitat filter. An overview must retain temporal context. Use calendar day as the time unit; brushing selects a half-open interval [start, end).

ID Day Habitat Value r1 1 Coast 10 r2 2 Ridge 20 r3 3 Coast 30 r4 4 Coast 40 r5 5 Ridge 50 r6 6 Coast missing r7 7 Ridge 70 r8 8 Coast 80

Required observations:

  • Brushing [2, 5) selects exactly r2, r3, r4. Day 5 is excluded. Reverse dragging produces the same set. Endpoint inclusion is visible in the range control or explanation.
  • Filtering to Coast retains three selected IDs, reports two selected records in the current filter, and exposes five eligible records. The selected visible value mean is 35, computed from r3, r4; the selection denominator is not silently replaced by the total corpus size.
  • The full Coast mean is 40 over four observed values, with one missing value separately accounted for. Missing does not become zero or disappear from the record count.
  • Pin r2, then filter to Coast. The pin remains identifiable with its hidden status, or the interface explicitly asks to replace it. Hovering r4 and leaving restores the pin; it does not commit a new selection.
  • Zooming the main chart changes the viewport and representation as needed, while the overview retains the full temporal domain and the three selected identities survive. Resetting the viewport does not clear the selection.
  • An empty brush has a visible zero-result state distinct from "no selection." Clearing the selection restores the declared unselected behavior.

docs.title: B. Document or image collection across scale
docs.text:
Brief: Build a collection browser for eight synthetic documents. At a broad scale show two collections and their composition; at a middle scale expose documents; close up, expose readable excerpts and metadata. Let a reader select documents, cross a tier boundary, inspect one, and return to the original place. Supply an equally capable linear route for keyboard use and small screens.

Use IDs d1–d4 in collection A and d5–d8 in collection B. Give d2 and d6 the same title, "Survey notes," but different excerpts. Give d4 a missing thumbnail. Initially select d2, d5, d8; pin d6. Filter out d8 in a later step. The contents are fixtures, not an asserted semantic clustering result.

Required observations:

  • Overview groups expose selection membership: A has 1/4 selected, B has 2/4. They cannot appear wholly selected. After filtering d8, show B's visible 1/3 selected alongside the fact that one selected document is hidden.
  • A tier change adds or replaces task-relevant representation: counts and summaries become recognizable document objects, then readable content. Enlarging thumbnails without adding meaningful content does not pass.
  • Selecting or pinning either duplicate title identifies the correct ID and excerpt in every view. Array position and display title are not identities.
  • Crossing the representation boundary back and forth preserves selected IDs, the pin, and the spatial anchor. If the focused DOM element is replaced, focus transfers to its semantic successor; it does not drop to the page body.
  • Slow movement around a threshold does not flicker between tiers. Returning from detail restores enough location context to find the same neighborhood.
  • The missing thumbnail has a usable identity and inspection route. Zooming does not trigger repeated unbounded image loads. Motion reduction preserves the state transition without requiring a flying camera.

Bounded ZUI navigation and return extension: Use the same collection as a two-dimensional space, with world bounds [0, 1600] × [0, 1000]. Place collection A near (300, 300) and B near (1200, 700), with the document positions stored in world coordinates. Start at a fitted overview; select d2, d5, d8 and pin d6. Record camera position, scale, focused entity, and navigation-history length at each action. Declare the allowed scale interval and camera-boundary policy before testing.

  • Anchored zoom: Choose an off-center point that is away from world bounds. Zoom by a factor of two and back using pointer, keyboard, and any offered pinch route. The same world point remains at the same screen location within a stated rendering tolerance, such as one CSS pixel. Check both axes; a horizontal chart-domain change cannot satisfy this collection task. Boundary clamping is separately visible and tested, rather than treated as anchor preservation.
  • Fit and Back: Pan to an asymmetric view, then inspect d2. Fit computes a camera that contains its declared target (document, collection, selection, or whole space). Back restores the recorded previous camera, including its offset and scale. They must produce distinct results in this fixture. Returning to the preceding location must not clear selection, change the pin, or replace a user's manually chosen camera with a newly fitted one.
  • Scale limits and history: At minimum and maximum scale, repeat the outward zoom action. It is a true no-op: the camera, selection, preview, pin, focus, and history length remain unchanged. One continuous gesture creates the declared single navigation checkpoint, not one entry per input event. Back must not require traversing invisible no-op entries.
  • Reflow and intentional position: Resize the host from a wide screen to a narrow one after an intentional pan. Preserve the declared world anchor or give a visible recovery action. Browser resize or delayed thumbnail arrival cannot silently refit the entire space. If the design offers a reflowing collection layout, record the world-to-entity correspondence before and after reflow and preserve the selected/pinned IDs; test reflow separately from camera navigation.
  • Preview and pin: Crossing the close-up threshold may reveal d2's content or initiate a preview under an explicit policy. It cannot pin d2 merely because the camera approached it. d6 remains pinned; zooming away removes a transient preview and restores the pinned detail. An explicit inspect/pin action remains available through keyboard controls.
  • Bounds and reachability: Pan toward all four corners and apply repeated large wheel or key inputs. The camera remains finite and obeys the declared bounded or elastic policy. Every document, including those near the edges, can still be reached and inspected at a readable scale. The overview and a keyboard recovery control can return from an empty region without requiring knowledge of the offscreen coordinates.
  • Focus continuity: Focus d2, cross every representation boundary, then return. Its semantic successor keeps focus and a visible indicator even if DOM nodes, canvas layers, or thumbnail representations change. If d2 becomes unavailable, focus moves to an explained collection or navigation target. Virtualization cannot send focus to the page body or leave it on an invisible recycled object.

This extension tests navigation of a collection. It does not require a new faceting runtime. When applying it to Wunderkammer, evaluate any existing filters or collection membership behavior against their own declared task and data contract; do not equate that behavior with camera movement.

docs.title: C. Heterogeneous linked data and non-bijective joins
docs.text:
Brief: Build a customer, order, and event investigation surface. Let a reader select a customer, inspect the related orders and events, and compare tags. The views have different units of analysis. Make unmatched data and count units visible. A shared x-axis is neither required nor meaningful.

Customers are c1, c2, c3. Orders are o1(c1, 10), o2(c1, 30), o3(c2, 20), and o4(no customer, 5). Events are e1(o1), e2(o1), e3(o2), e4(o3), and e5(unknown order). Tag A relates to o1, o2; tag B relates to o2, o3.

Required observations:

  • Selecting c1 links to exactly two orders totaling 40 and three events. The second event on o1 does not count its order amount again.
  • Selecting both tags yields three distinct orders, not four. Any weighted or multiplicity-based metric is separately named and justified.
  • Selecting c3 yields no related orders and visibly empty target views. Clearing that selection restores all records; the two actions are distinct.
  • o4 and e5 remain discoverable as unmatched records. A join cannot silently drop them while claiming to show the entire input dataset.
  • The source entity and join direction are intelligible. Selecting event e1 may link to o1 and c1, but any expansion to sibling event e2 is explicitly defined and visually distinguishable from the original selected entity.
  • Sorting, filtering, and aggregate expansion do not change identity mapping. The rendered count labels name customers, orders, or events as appropriate.

docs.title: D. Geographic and temporal views with independent navigation
docs.text:
Brief: Build an observation map linked to a timeline and record list. Select observations in either view, inspect their correspondence, and inspect a dense map region without losing the global time context. The map has longitude and latitude; the timeline has dates. Declare how multiple selections combine.

Use five records: p1(-5, 0, day 1), p2(0, 0, day 2), p3(5, 0, day 3), p4(0, 5, day 4), p5(5, 5, day 5). Define the test rectangle as -1 <= longitude <= 1 and -1 <= latitude <= 6, which yields p2, p4. Define the time brush [2, 4), which yields p2, p3.

Required observations:

  • Replace produces the most recent set; add produces p2, p3, p4; intersection produces p2; subtracting the time set from the map set produces p4. Offer only operators the interface declares, and test each offered operator.
  • Map navigation changes the map viewport without changing timeline scale or turning pan into selection. The selected IDs remain shared.
  • Pixel-to-data conversion works when the plot begins away from the document origin, the page is scrolled, and the graphic is CSS-scaled. Nested transforms and SVG viewBox letterboxing must be covered when the host uses them.
  • Small-screen interaction has an explicit way to choose navigation versus brushing. Touch scrolling outside the plot still works; multiple pointers do not silently commit the first pointer's unfinished selection.

docs.title: Adversarial interaction sequences
docs.text:
Run applicable cases against every built artifact, not only a purpose-built test harness. A feature absent from the product is not applicable, with the reason recorded; an offered but untested feature is not observed.

Sequence Observable invariant Start a replacement brush, move outside the plot, press Escape The prior committed set survives; transient geometry disappears; keyboard focus remains usable Start a brush, then pointercancel / loss of capture / window blur No unfinished selection commits; capture and temporary listeners are released Draw a nonzero rectangle that contains no marks, then clear Explicit empty selection and absence of selection remain distinguishable Click or tap without crossing the drag threshold The documented click action occurs; no accidental empty brush replaces the selection Start from {a,b}; add {b,c}; subtract {b}; undo if offered Sets become {a,b,c}, then {a,c}; undo restores exactly the preceding committed state Preview A while B is pinned; move to empty space or another view Preview clears through the shared path and B remains pinned Change a filter while records are selected offscreen Selection identity and visibility counts agree; filtered or offscreen records are not confused with deleted records Change data revision during a pending brush The gesture is cancelled or recomputed under an explicit policy; IDs from incompatible revisions cannot be committed silently Issue request A, then B; resolve B before A Visible results stay on B; a stale A response cannot repaint them or restore its selection Change viewport while a selection overlay exists The overlay reprojects from its declared domain or IDs; stale screen coordinates do not change meaning Resize or cross a semantic tier while a child control has focus Focus has a visible, relevant destination and remains operable Remove a selected or pinned record from the data The missing identity is explained or cleared according to a visible policy; another row cannot inherit it

Async, deleted-data, and multi-pointer cases require host fixtures; a static reference lab cannot establish them. Do not retrofit a fake loading spinner to claim asynchronous verification.

docs.title: Narrow routing counterexamples
docs.text:
These briefs test restraint. Use fresh sessions and inspect the runnable result or proposal; checking whether the agent mentions "brush" is not a valid test.

Brief Expected decision and evidence "Fix the spacing of the already specified zoom buttons; behavior is approved" Follow the host's settled control model; no new selection or linking system "Show the latest total and its units on a status page" A readable direct display; no invented exploratory canvas or selection state "Add a date filter to this appointment form" A conventional bounded input is sufficient unless a concrete distribution-comparison task is supplied "Make this static publication figure readable when printed" Work through the figure channel and print constraints; no interaction required to interpret the export "The gallery's image magnifier must show the original pixels" Geometric magnification preserves the requested content; semantic substitution is not imposed "Build three independent operational controls with unrelated data" Preserve independent state; shared appearance alone does not warrant cross-filtering

For a paired positive test, add a genuine relationship task to the last brief: "Choose a deployment and inspect its errors, hosts, and traces." The response should then define correspondence and linked state. This tests whether routing responds to task meaning rather than surface nouns.

docs.title: Human comparison when an outcome claim matters
docs.text:
The following is a study plan, not evidence that these mechanisms improve performance. Start with observed workflow failures and a relevant existing interface. Pick tasks that both conditions can complete, and preserve data, labels, available information, and answer criteria across conditions.

  1. Define the claim and task before recruiting. For example: find which habitat changed within a time window, recover a previously inspected record, or explain why an aggregate includes certain members. Decide which task tests correspondence, navigation, selection, or learning. Do not claim a general cognitive benefit from one successful task.
  2. Choose the comparison that addresses the mechanism. Compare the host's current interface with the proposed one. If separating zoom from linking matters, use a targeted variant or staged comparison. Keep the baseline capable and equally polished; otherwise the result cannot isolate the mechanism. A factorial study is useful only when the research question and participant budget support it.
  3. Separate learning from practiced performance. Capture unassisted first use, provide the same amount of instruction, then use parallel datasets for practiced trials. Counterbalance condition and task order. Use different values with comparable structure to reduce answer memorization. A delayed retention task is needed for a retention claim.
  4. Define denominators and failures. Report correct task answers / assigned tasks, participants completing each condition / recruited participants, recoveries / induced recoverable errors, and condition-specific missingness. Measure elapsed time from an explicit start to an explicit completion. Report incomplete tasks and timeouts alongside time for successful tasks; do not hide them in a faster-successes-only mean.
  5. Observe the mechanism. Record chosen IDs, operations, tier crossings, resets, accidental selections, backtracks, and help requests alongside task correctness. Think-aloud can reveal confusion but changes task timing; use a separate session or acknowledge that limit. Logs alone do not reveal why a person acted.
  6. Treat insight tasks carefully. Collect an answer and its cited data. Define valid findings and scoring examples beforehand; blind raters to condition where practical. Report agreement, unsupported findings, duplicates, and findings per participant within a fixed observation period. Verbosity or number of interactions is not an insight measure.
  7. Recruit for the claimed population and input modes. Include relevant domain experience and access needs. Test keyboard, screen reader, or touch with people who use them before making claims about their usability. Use pilot variance and a smallest meaningful effect to plan a comparative sample; a convenient small pilot supports defect discovery, not a universal ranking.
  8. Report uncertainty and scope. Analyze paired observations as paired when appropriate, account for repeated tasks per participant, and report effect estimates with uncertainty. Predeclare primary outcomes and exclusions when testing a performance claim. Preserve contradictions: improved speed with worse accuracy or harder first use is a tradeoff, not an overall win.

docs.title: Evidence receipt
docs.text:
Attach a compact record to a completed evaluation:

Skill and artifact revisions:
Brief, dataset version, and expected answers:
Host browser, viewport, device/input mode:
Model cases passed / failed / not observed:
Real input cases passed / failed / not observed:
Rendered states inspected and captures:
Human participants, assigned tasks, completed tasks (if any):
First reproducible defect and its consequence:
Claim supported by this evidence:
Unverified boundaries and next check:

Do not mark the battery complete merely because the reference example passes. Keep a new failing build as a regression fixture when it exposes a transferable skill or implementation defect.

docs.title: Polish rules — UI micro-interaction + visual-detail discipline
docs.text:
Load this detailed reference only when the compact polish channel points to an exact rule or the task needs a comprehensive implementation or audit pass.

The frontend-polish channel: the codified design-engineering rules that turn an OK interface into one that feels considered. Concentric border radius. Optical alignment. Scale on press. Tabular numbers. Interruptible transitions. The small things that compound.

This is distinct from sibling channels:

  • channels/web.md covers editorial HTML, Marginalia, Pandoc, and static capture — the prose surface.
  • channels/interactive.md covers live demos where the reader moves parameters — the exploratory surface.
  • This channel covers UI polish — the tactile surface that any frontend benefits from regardless of its higher-level purpose.

Structurally mined from thedavidmurray/claude-make-interfaces-feel-better (MIT, archived 2026-05). The 16 rules below are ported and tightened for muriel's brand floor; per-rule citations live inline. Mining stance follows muriel's curator pattern — port the discipline, not the React component code.

Part of the muriel skill — see the top-level index for mission, universal rules, and channel map.

docs.title: When to use
docs.text:
• Building or reviewing UI components (buttons, cards, dropdowns, modals)
  • Implementing animations, hover states, shadows, borders, typography micro-details
  • Reviewing AI-generated frontend code for "feels off" without obvious cause
  • Adding tactile feedback (scale on press, hover lift)
  • Closing the gap between "renders correctly" and "feels considered"
  • Triggers: "make it feel better", "polish this", "feels off", "jarring", "loose"

If the work is data viz, use channels/charts.md. If it's a live demo, use channels/interactive.md. If it's prose-rendering HTML, use channels/web.md.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
1. Identify the surface. Is it a button, card, list item, modal, navigation? Different surfaces apply different subsets of rules.
  2. Apply universal rules (1–4 below) — they hit nearly every interface.
